audits.title: Illegal Imports of products of animal origin and live animals

recommendations.text: Competent authorities The FAVV/AFSCA is responsible for the import controls at the BIPs. The Customs authorities are "Federale Overheidsdienst Financien/Service Public Fédéral Finances" within the "Ministry of Finance", and they execute import controls for freight and supervise BIP and non-BIP crossing points for personal baggage checks, non-commercial pet animals, and check amongst their other tasks for illegal imports of veterinary products and live animals. Customs is also responsible for checks on products and live animals listed in the Annexes to Council Regulation (EC) No 338/97(e) (CITES).

Legislative and administrative measures The CCA stated that EU Regulations and Decisions are directly applicable without the need for national publication. ¾ Responsibilities for the checks according to Commission Regulation (EC) No 745/2004 and Regulation (EC) No 998/2003(f) have been defined. ¾ Two airport-entry-points are considered to be relevant according to Regulation (EC) No 745/2004; however, passenger transport, in particular for interline passengers, cannot be excluded through other entry points as five airports have the status "international airports". ¾ There is no official list of entry points for pet animals according to Regulation (EC) No 998/2003; CCA stated, that three airports are considered as entry- points for pet animals. Customs are responsible for checks on pet animals; however, as customs are not equipped accordingly, were not trained and do not have instructions, the checks are delegated to be carried out by BIP-staff. ¾ National instructions to customs were outdated and no specific administrative procedures have been put in place for implementing the two above mentioned Regulations or for specifying sanctions. Draft instructions prepared by BIP staff in some border crossing points were sent to the customs. ¾ No specific information (e.g. third country lists or information on animal disease situation in third countries) has been provided to customs. 2 ¾ The CCA did contact airline companies to inform passengers of the requirements foreseen in Regulation (EC) No 745/2004(2).

Co-operation between different authorities ¾ At central level co-operation of FAVV with customs has improved, however, no formal co-operation agreements between the services are in place. The veterinary services do not have access to customs databases. ¾ The positive list of Commission Decision 2002/349/EC(g) has been sent to customs; it has not been sent to port and airport authorities, which are not aware of the requirements, as the Decision has not been published. ¾ No general overview was available of the number and quantity of illegally imported consignments of animal origin and live animals seized by customs in all entry points. ¾ Co-operation with port and airport authorities is not efficient; posters have been submitted to the airports but not to ports and no overview was available as to whether posters had been displayed in the airport ­ entry-points and if so, how many. ¾ Customs on the local level are not always aware of the requirements of the positive list and the requirements in the national customs instructions provided in paper form were outdated. 5.2. CHECKS ON ILLEGAL IMPORTS "Illegal imports" in the context of this report, is the introduction onto the territory of the Community of products of animal origin or live animals which, either accidentally or intentionally, have not been subject to, and cleared following, the veterinary checks foreseen in Community legislation. 5.2.1. Organisation and operation of Customs ¾ There are no specific measures in place or specific staff allocated for the detection of illegal imports and customs checks on personal luggage for illegal imports are part of their general tasks and their main focus is on fiscal issues. ¾ Checks on personal baggage are carried out based on customs risk assessment and highest priority is assigned to Brussel-Zaventem, in particular for flights originating in Africa and South East Asia. ¾ No system is in place to ensure that customs have current information to use in their risk assessment in relation to the animal disease risk posed by third countries. ¾ The general customs rules provide for the possibility to place goods for a certain time in temporary storage. The freight can remain for 45 days in the ports and for 20 days in the airports before the request for customs approved treatment has to be made. ¾ In the customs databases used for free release of consignments ("SADBEL" and "TARBEL") not all relevant CN-codes were linked with the requirements (2) In their comments to the draft report the Belgian CCA clarified that a meeting between the CCA and various airline companies had been held on 30.08.2004 with the conclusion that CCA awaits a reply form the Airlines Operating Committee as regards the possibility of informing passengers. 3 for veterinary checks, see also findings under point 5.2.6 in report DG(SANCO)/7647/2005. The customs database used for customs transit procedures (NCTS) does not contain a link to veterinary checks; however, customs may check in their instructions. ¾ Customs stated in relation to CITES products and live animals that in case of doubts they inform the relevant BIP. 5.2.2. Imports of products for personal consumption 5.2.2.1.Background Customs are responsible for personal baggage checks of travellers in all points of entry and they also carry out daily checks in the centres for mail and express mail. ¾ No specific training was provided in the field of veterinary checks and checks for illegal imports of veterinary consignments. 5.2.2.2.Information to passengers/travellers ¾ The big posters displayed in the BIP-airport- and a non-BIP-airport-entry-point visited contained all the information foreseen in Regulation (EC) No 745/2004. Small posters displayed in one BIP-airport were outdated. ¾ No further initiatives were taken in order to increase public awareness as no information reflecting the provisions of the above Regulation is distributed to the passengers in aircrafts or ships. Although one BIP contacted airline operators in 2001 to inform passengers, nothing happened and no further follow up took place. Thus, it was not ensured that airline operators or shipping lines inform their passengers accordingly; e.g. no in-flight-announcements are made. 5.2.2.3.Organisation of controls/sanctions ¾ Customs are permanently present in the points of entry from third countries, either BIPs or non-BIPs. Customs stated that in case of the airports all arriving flights from third countries in all points of entry are checked and international flights from other EU airports are checked in a similar way as the passengers come through the same channel. ¾ In this framework no priority is given to veterinary products as these are included in the general illegal imports checks. Customs stated that checks are carried out for all illegal imports on a risk based approach. The criteria for risk analyses varied between flights from different countries and personal experience of customs officers. Thus, for each point of entry individual criteria are applicable. ¾ Customs did not receive the relevant and updated information concerning products of animal origin allowed to be imported without veterinary checks as required in Art. 1 of Regulation (EC) No 745/2004. ¾ Passengers are neither liable for the cost of destruction of seized consignments nor for any penalties laid down in Art. 4 of Regulation (EC) No 745/2004, if the illegal consignments are abandoned or seized after being discovered by customs. Customs stated that it is practically difficult to request financial contributions from travellers with an address in Africa. ¾ Customs reported that passengers express strong resentment of the checks performed mainly due to the lack of awareness of the passenger to what is allowed to enter the EU. 4 ¾ Information according to Art. 5 of Regulation (EC) No 745/2004 has been submitted to the relevant Commission services, however it is not complete as information is not included from all entry points where seizures take place. BIP-airport-entry-points: ¾ Regarding veterinary products at a major BIP-airport-entry-point flights from African and the Far East countries have the highest priority to be checked for products for personal consumption whereas in another BIP-airport-entry-point all flights originating from third countries are checked. ¾ No additional resources had been made available for checks on personal luggage for Brussel-Zaventem and in case of flights arriving early in the morning from high risk countries, these cannot be controlled due to the limited staffing in the night shift (day shift: 7 -8 officers, night shift: 2 ­ 3 officers). ¾ As part of their integrated controls customs checks physically about 10 % of luggage from all flights from third countries. According to the information provided in the major BIP-airport-entry-point 10,895 kg of meat and milk products were seized by customs in 2004, however, on-the-spot it was stated, that mostly fish products were seized. In another BIP-airport-entry-point in 2004 there were 152 passengers checked and 5 kg meat were found. In the third BIP-airport-entry-point about 100 ­ 150 passengers per plane were checked and no products of animal origin were found. ¾ Customs stated that interline luggage of passengers from third countries with stopover in other EU airports is checked at the destination airport in Belgium. No lists of the arriving passengers are received and the physical luggage check is based on random selection at the green channel from the colour-coded tags of the luggage. ¾ In a Belgium main airport 100 % interline luggage is scanned for security reasons. ¾ Sniffer dogs are not trained to check for products of animal origin. Customs use X-ray-scanning equipment to check selected baggage; however, no data were available. No mass screening is performed on baggage. ¾ Seizures are also criteria for the risk analysis carried out by customs and the only detailed overview of results of checks was available in Brussel-Zaventem, which enables a more risk based approach for targeting checks. ¾ The seized consignments were collected in specific boxes or containers under customs control; however, there were no amnesty bins for passengers voluntarily abandoning products of animal origin. Customs stated that passengers have the possibility to hand over relevant products to customs, which never happened. ¾ Seized consignments are incinerated; however, customs could not provide confirmation for their adequate disposal and there was no list of establishments approved under Regulation (EC) No 1774/2002(h). Furthermore, in Liège the collecting document referred to category 3 waste, which is not in accordance with requirements in the above mentioned Regulation. At a non-BIP-airport-entry-point: there are no regular direct flights for third countries. Only private flights could arrive, mainly from Russia and Switzerland. 5 ¾ Instructions for checking products of animal origin and live animals used by customs are not updated since 1993. Not all CN-codes are linked to the requirements for veterinary control. ¾ Customs use scanning equipment to check luggage. There are no sniffer dogs trained for products of animal origin. ¾ Customs indicated that certain difficulties occur in ensuring that passengers luggage is submitted to customs control. Illegal introduction of products of animal origin can therefore not fully be excluded. 5.2.3. Import and transit of freight ¾ The selection of the consignments subject to veterinary checks is not completely reliable and consignments may escape veterinary checks as relevant customs databases do not fully integrate the requirements for veterinary checks, in particular for consignments under customs transit procedure, see also findings under point 5.2.6 in report DG(SANCO)/7647/2005. ¾ At one medium sized BIP-airport-entry point almost 10 % of the general cargo consignments are customs released for free circulation and a 100 % documentary check is carried out. Based on the risk analysis (origin of goods, importer, declarant, itinerary, product, customs destination) around 2,5 - 3 % of these consignments are physically checked. No scanners are used. No veterinary goods were detected which were not declared as such in 2004. For 90 % of the general cargo consignments a customs transit procedure is assigned, and 1 % of these are physically checked. The percentage of these checks is attributed by the "SADBEL-system", however, additional checks may be carried out by a specific monitoring team. Customs indicated that their priority lies in the collection of the duties. Non-BIP-airport-entry point: ¾ There is no freight traffic by airplane; however, consignments are received from other airports by road. They arrive by truck with an air waybill and the customs procedure for free circulation or further transit is requested in Antwerpen airport. There are no such consignments with products of animal origin received during the past 2 - 3 years. ¾ Customs stated that 2,588 declarations for free circulation were opened in 2004, on which in 100 % a documentary check is carried out and 5 % of them are checked physically. 1,679 consignments were destined for customs transit procedure in 2003 and no physical check is carried out for these at the airport. ¾ Approximately 10 - 15 personal shipments per month are customs released for free circulation. Consignments originating from Nigeria are prioritised for physical checks according to the local risk profile and about 70 % of them are physically checked. ¾ No wrongly declared products of animal origin were found by customs in 2004. ¾ Since 1996 there were no seizures under CITES-Regulations. BIP-port-entry points: ¾ After the customs approved treatment is requested, 100 % of the consignments for release for free circulation are subjected to documentary checks. Physical checks are based on the risk analysis taking into consideration the importer, type of goods and their origin, history and flow of traffic. The "SADBEL- 6 system" selects consignments for physical checks based on the risk criteria contained in the system. Local customs units can add additional criteria for the selection of consignments for physical control. They can vary between 0,5 to 3 % depending on the type of documentation and economic customs procedures. ¾ Due to the location of the BIP-facilities in a different customs designated area of the port in Antwerpen than the arrival of the consignments, a customs approved treatment (free circulation or transit) has to be assigned before the consignments are transported to the BIP. After the veterinary inspection the hard copy of the customs documents has to be stamped in the designated customs verification office. 70 consignments were moved from the port in 2004 without verification in the designated customs verification office and it was not clarified, if veterinary consignments were involved, which bypassed the BIP, see also point 5.2.6 of report DG(SANCO)/7647/2005. ¾ In Zeebrugge, during the physical checks carried out by customs, no products of animal origin not declared as such were found and in Antwerpen, out of 38 cases, five consignments with products of animal origin were found, of which one was declared as such. ¾ There were around 723,479 declarations for free circulation in 2003 in Antwerpen. 352 cases were found in 2004, for which incorrect declarations have been inserted in the customs database. ¾ For consignments under customs transit procedure, very limited physical checks (two for each 1,000 consignments/at least four each month) are carried out in the port of arrival. For incorrect declarations in the NCTS-system, no figures were available. ¾ There is one scanner in Antwerpen port and it is planned to install a second one in May 2005. In Zeebrugge, there are no scanners but they can request one from Antwerpen, which happened during the last two years for seven specific actions.

Import of live animals ¾ No specific guidelines have been issued to customs in relation to checks on pet animals and the services on-the-spot were not aware of the requirements. ¾ Information in the handbook referred to outdated requirements. ¾ No technical equipment such as micro-chip readers was available in the relevant entry-points. ¾ In one major BIP-airport-entry-point three cases (eagles and frogs) were discovered in 2004 as attempted illegal import. CCAs were not aware of other cases during the mission.

Import of post consignments Customs are permanently present in the express post service in Brussel­Zaventem, which is one point of entry for express mail, packages or parcels. ¾ Live animals cannot to be sent by post under the "Postal Convention" but for products of animal origin no specific restriction exists, except the positive list, which was provided by BIP staff to the entry point. ¾ Four hours before arrival of the consignments, a shipment list of all parcels is electronically provided and BIP staff also has access to this information. 7 ¾ The electronic system of the company contains a specific query to select parcels for veterinary control. According to the description of the consignment as meat, milk, fish etc. and the country of origin (23 countries are targeted, all for which safeguard decisions exist) a query is run; its results are reviewed to filter out non-relevant consignments. The relevant ones are blocked in the system and the consignments are moved to a specific place. Only customs have the power to un-block these consignments after checks have been carried out. ¾ Around 80 consignments per month of this selection are physically checked by BIP staff. Fish products of less then 1 kg are allowed for importation. Shipments with more then 1 kg fish products are re-dispatched to the country of origin. Meat and milk products are seized and send for destruction under category 2-regime. There is no statistic available of seized and destroyed consignments; however, the week before the mission live animals were found ¾ According to their risk analysis, customs can block additional parcels. Every month customs change the criteria for their risk analysis. There is no specific focus on products of animal origin at present, but could be included if considered as a risk. ¾ The main criteria to check express mail, packages or parcels is the value. Consignments of more then 22 Euro value move under T 1-procedure to a customs warehouse and are checked and customs cleared there. From consignments below 22 Euro, around 0,14 % per day are physically checked by customs. Customs stated that they never found products of animal origin which were not declared as such. ¾ A scanner is available but used rarely by customs. There are no sniffer dogs, which would be not considered to be useful due to the technology of sorting the parcels. ¾ 40 shipments (39,86 kg) of products of animal origin (dried fish meat and poultry meat), mainly from Hong-Kong, China, Thailand and Burundi were seized in 2005. ¾ Twice a month seized parcels are send for destruction, however there is no separation between products of animal origin and other waste to be destroyed. All waste is classified under code 020203. The weight send for destruction is different from the weight received at the incinerator and no conformation of destruction is received. BIP staff, who carry out the physical checks twice/week, stated that in a mail/parcel sorting centre nearby a similar system has been put in place and that the checks carried out are based on the country of origin. However, the veterinarian cannot open the mail without the presence of customs.

audits.title: Controls on Feed and compliance with requirements for Feed Hygiene

recommendations.text: To ensure that all staff has the appropriate training enabling them to undertake their duties competently as required by Art. 6 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.
To finalize efforts to put a system in place to verify the effectiveness of official controls as required by Art. 8(3) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. With regard to official controls on feed
To ensure that official controls cover all stages of production, processing and distribution of feed as required by Art. 3.3 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, in particular as regards hauliers.

To ensure that for the organisation of official controls identified risks and operators past records on compliance are always taken into account as required by Art. 3.1 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.
To ensure efficient and effective coordination at all levels of the CCA as required by Art. 4.3. of Regulation 882/2004, in particular with regard to the provincial level.

To ensure that requirements of Art. 2 of Directive 98/68/EC are complied with and that efficient and effective coordination is always ensured between the CCA and the customs authorities as required by Art. 4(3) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.
To provide other MS with administrative assistance such as information about dispatched feedingstuffs only allowed for export, as outlined in Art. 34 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

To ensure the appropriate follow-up of non-compliant results of comparative tests organised to verify the reliability of the laboratory network involved in feed controls in order to be in line with Art. 33 (2) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. With regard to compliance with requirements for feed hygiene
To publish an updated list, or lists, of registered and approved FBOs as required by Art. 19 of Regulation (EC) No 183/2005.

To ensure that all relevant FBOs are registered according to their activities as required by Art. 9 of Regulation (EC) No 183/2005, in particular at primary production level and for food business operators supplying the feed chain. __________________ 12 COMPETENT AUTHORITY RESPONSE TO RECOMMENDATIONS

audits.title: GMO - Controls on food and feed

recommendations.text: The annual programme for food and feed will be adopted in the course of the last trimester of 2006 and will be send to the UCP. It will clearly indicate sampling at, amongst others, entry points.

The general protocol of cooperation of customs and the AFSCA is foreseen to be finalised until end of 2006. The adoption of the protocol will permit planning of import controls for GM food and feed, which will be part of the control plan for 2007.

In relation to the sampling plan for 2007, instructions are under preparation for controls at BIPs and at entry points for food and feed potentially containing GMO, taking into account Commissio 2004/787/EC.

audits.title: Pesticides

recommendations.text: In accordance with Article 17 of Directive 91/414/EEC, the competent authorities should consider introducing controls on marketing and use of PPPs extended to cover all sellers and users.
The competent authority should ensure that complete reports of the control activities on marketing and use are sent to the Commission according to Article 17 of Directive 91/414/EEC.
The competent authority should take appropriate measures to ensure that adequate communication and co-operation is established between the two services for controls of marketing and use of PPPs.

The competent authorities should consider taking full account of the Quality Control Procedures for Pesticide Residues Analysis Document No. SANCO/10476/2003, particularly with respect to routine recovery.

In accordance with Article 17.2 of Regulation 178/2002, it should be ensured that the quantification limits meet the requirements of EU MRL legislation, particularly with respect to Commission Directives 91/321/EEC and 96/5/EC on foodstuffs for infants and young children. 19 An action plan in response to the recommendations should be forwarded to the Commission within 2 months of dispatch of the final translated report. This action plan should clearly set out the manner and deadline by which the competent authorities will address each recommendation. 9. ADDENDUM In their comments to the draft report, the Belgian authorities submitted a preliminary response to the recommendations. With regard to recommendation (1) the competent authorities stated that AFSCA already controls all PPP sellers and FPS-Public Health will organise more systematic controls of professional users. Concer (2) the competent authorities stated that results of controls performed by the FPS-Public Health will also be reported to the Commission. Regardi (3) a collaboration protocol is planned to be drafted between the AFSCA and the FPS- Public Health to specify the tasks of each body and clarify, in particular, aspects relating to overlapping of control activities, and to coordination and communication. In relation to recommendation (4), the competent authorities stated that the new document "Quality Control Procedures for Pesticide Residues Analysis" (SANCO/10232/2006) will be applied. Finally, in relation to recommendation (5) the competent authorities stated that laboratories designated for the analysis of foodstuffs for infants and young children will tailor their performance to the MRLs established in the legislation.

audits.title: Food Hygiene - Food of animal origin

recommendations.text: Ensure as soon as possible that the system for the control of operators' activities, introduced this year, is operational and effective, taking special account of the following elements: the uniform evaluation of observations, the request for corrective action, the setting of deadlines, monitoring and the application of penalties.

audits.title: Import controls for plant health

recommendations.text: Plant health checks are only carried out at places that have the appropriate minimum conditions specified in the Annexes to Directives 98/22/EC and 2004/103/EC as required by Article 1 and Article 1(2) of the same Directives.

Notifications of interception are made available to Commission and other Member States within two days, or preferably sooner in the case of a refusal, as required by Article 2 of Directive 94/3/EC of the interception.

The responsible official bodies in charge of the inspection posts have up-to-date information on consignments of plants and plant products coming from third countries which have undergone official interception, in accordance with Article 1 of Directive 98/22/EC.

The plant health checks are sufficient, especially with regards to the proportion of each consignment inspected, to determine that consignments of plants and plant products are not contaminated by harmful organisms, and that they comply with the relevant special requirements listed in Annex IV of Directive 2000/29/EC, as required by Articles 13(1)(i) and 13a (1)(a) of the same Directive.

The points of entry authorised for the introduction of potatoes from Egypt and the name and address of the responsible official body in charge of each point is notified to the Commission in accordance with point 1(c) of the Annex to Decision 2004/4/EC.
Consignments are always accompanied by documents that comply with the requirements of Article 13(1)(ii) of Directive 2000/29/EC. The Single Authority in Belgium is advised to consider:
Issuing guidance on the proportion of each consignment that should be inspected for plant health purposes to ensure an appropriate probability of finding any harmful organisms present.

Issuing instructions or guidelines for performing checks for the presence of non- declared or prohibited items in consignments. The Single Authority is invited to provide, within 25 working days of receipt of the report, an action plan containing details of the actions taken and planned, including deadlines for their completion, to address the above recommendations. 10. audits.title: Animal health - live animals - intracommunity trade; identification, registration, sheep & goats

recommendations.text: Discontinue the certification at cattle dealers' premises, which does not comply with Article 5(2) of Directive 64/432/EEC.

Revise the conditions for certifying cattle so as to certify only at authorised assembly centres or holdings of origin, in accordance with Article 5(2) of Directive 64/432/EEC ­Revise the assembly centre procedures to ensure that all cattle and pigs accepted have the same health status, in accordance with Article 11(1)(a) of Directive 64/432/EEC; Allow only animals accompanied by an official document containing all the necessary information, and concerning the holding of origin, to be certified at assembly centres in accordance with Article 5(2)(b) of Directive 64/432/EEC.

Revise the approvals of assembly centres and dealers' premises to ensure that they are properly granted under the relevant legislation and meet the conditions of Articles 11 and 13 of Directive 64/432/EEC or Articles 8a and 8b of Directive 91/68/EEC. Transmit the list of duly approved assembly centres to the Commission in accordance with Commission Decision 2007/468/EC; Similarly revise the approvals of inspection posts (staging points) and send to the Commission the updated lists of approved points in accordance with Article 3(1) of Regulation (EC) No 1255/97. 4

Revise the requirements and apply and inspect correctly all standards for the notification and monitoring of cattle movements for all keepers (in passports, registers and the database), in accordance with the relevant provisions of Article 14C of Directive 64/432/EEC (particularly point 1, 7th indent, and Article 7(3) of Regulation (EC) No 1760/2000 and Chapter II of Regulation (EC) No 911/2004, Articles 6 and 8); apply the same to inspections of sheep and goat movements (systematic use of the circulation documents described, complete records containing all data in Annex B.1 of Regulation (EC) No 21/2004); ensure that the data field for health information enables restrictions on movements and other relevant information to be entered in accordance with point D.1 of the annex to Regulation (EC) No 21/2004 and Article 1(1)(e) of Decision 2000/678/EC.

Ensure that the regular inspections of dealers under Article 13(4) of Directive 64/432/EEC or Article 8b(4) of Directive 91/68/EC guarantee that activities as dealers are clearly separated from activities as production or rearing holdings.

Revise the identification of pigs at the assembly centre so as to register them in such a way that the original or transit holding, centre or organisation can be traced, in accordance with Article 3(1)© of Directive 90/425/EEC.

Ensure that the certification of equidae is also based on the declarations of the owner or keeper, under Article 4(2) of Directive 90/426/EEC, whose name is mentioned in the passport in accordance with requirement II.1 of the annex to Decision 93/623/EEC, and whose holding is registered in accordance with Article 6(2) of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004, where equidae are not excluded from the food chain.

Ensure that, in accordance with Article 6 of Directive 90/426/EEC, derogations from inspections prior to intra-Community trade in equidae granted to other Member States are notified to the Commission.

Revise the certification procedures to ensure that all certification points are checked and documented. Revise the conditions for the training and supervision of certifying veterinarians so as to ensure that they understand the implications of Directive 96/93/EC.

Revise the procedures for issuing certificates, notification in TRACES and certificate checking so as to guarantee the correct and complete communication of the certified data, the date of issue of the certificate and the information to the Member State of destination, in accordance with Article 4(2) of Directive 90/425/EEC.
Revise and check the procedures for entering Part III of certificates in Traces where a check is undertaken, in accordance with Article 3(2)(a) of Decision 2004/292/EC.
Revise the regulations to ensure compulsory immediate notification of all diseases listed in Annex A of Directive 90/426/EEC.
Draw up, apply and check the standards of protection against attacks by the bluetongue vector at inspection posts, in accordance with Article 9(1)(c) of Regulation (EC) No 1266/2007. 5

Revise the protocols for inspecting the use of disinfectants so as to ensure that only disinfectants authorised by the competent authority are used for disinfecting means of animal transport and in places approved by the competent authority, in accordance with Article 12 of Directive 64/432/EEC, Article 8c of Directive 91/68/EEC and Article 7 of Directive 90/426/EEC. Ensure that all authorised disinfectants are labelled with an expiry date relevant to normal conditions of storage, in accordance with Article 20(3)(i) of Directive 98/8/EC. 6

audits.title: Import/Transit Control system and Border Inspection Posts

recommendations.text: To ensure that sufficient training is provided for all BIP staff in the specific areas where shortcomings had been noted such as physical checks on live animals (Annex to Decision 97/794/EC) or supervision of ship suppliers (Artt. 12 and 13 of Directive 97/78/EC and Decision 2001/571/EC).

To ensure that sufficient training is provided for all customs staff for the requirements of Regulation (EC) No 206/2009 and Regulation (EC) 998/2003 in order to fully implement the EU requirement for checks on passenger luggage and non-commercial pet animals.
To ensure that the import/transit control system and the listed BIPs are included in the programme of audits foreseen under Art. 4 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

To complete the scope of supervision undertaken with regard to official controls of BIPs and of Customs, and to establish a procedure to follow up shortcomings noted for the effectiveness of these controls, in order to fully complete verification of official controls and to ensure effectiveness of corrective actions as required by Art. 8 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

To further strengthen the existing co-operation with respect to arrangements for an exchange of relevant information available in the electronic systems of other authorities as provided for in Regulation (EC) No 136/2004 and Artt. 5 and 6 of Regulation (EC) No 282/2004.

To complete transposition of Artt. 12 (4) and 13 of Directive 97/78/EC with regard to approval of customs warehouses and authorisation of ship supplier in order to give effectiveness to administrative measures implemented to ensure that operators fulfil all their legal obligations with respect to this Directive.

To provide or update detailed instructions for the areas which at present are not specifically addressed or updated in order to ensure the correct application of the all veterinary procedures of the import/transit control system, in particular for supervision of authorised ship suppliers (Art. 13 of Directive 97/78/EC), for physical checks on live animals at BIPs (Annex to Decision 97/794/EC) and for the new requirements for checks on passenger luggage (Regulation (EC) No 206/2009).
To further improve the input of information into TRACES, required by Decision 2004/292/EC, in order to avoid confusing statistics in TRACES.

To further improve the system in place to follow up of incoming transit consignments in order to ensure that confirmation regarding arrival to warehouses or regarding exit of consignments is received within the 30 days time limit required in Art. 2 of Decision 2000/571/EC and Art. 11 (2) (c) of Directive 97/78/EC.

To ensure that documentary checks are carried out for consignments from third countries being transhipped to other third countries staying in a port more than seven and less than 20 days as required in Artt. 11 and 9 of Directive 97/78/EC.

To carry out checks on transit consignments at the BIP of exit in order to ensure the implementation of the requirements of Art. 11 (2) (e) of Directive 97/78/EC and Art. 3 of Decision 2000/208 for all exiting consignments.
To implement a procedure for authorisation of ship suppliers as required in Art. 13 (1) (a) of Directive 97/78/EC and Decision 2000/571/EC.

To further improve and co-ordinate between the different services the supervision of ship suppliers in order to ensure, that all requirements of Art. 13 of Directive 97/78/EC and Decision 2000/571/EC are fulfilled, the relevant findings are followed up and the approval document issued for the establishment reflects the activities of the operator.
To provide all relevant information of animal health risks to Customs in order to further improve their risk assessment for controls on passenger luggage.

To update instructions in place, to provide information to passengers and to finalise procedures for parcels send by post, to ensure that all requirements of Regulation (EC) No 206/2009 are complied with.

To ensure that commercial express parcel containing POAO or live animals are allowed for free circulation only if they are presented for veterinary checks to a BIP at the first place of entry into EU territory as required in Art. 4 (1) of Directive 91/496/EEC and Art. 3 (1) of Directive 97/78/EC.

To improve the system in place to check non-commercial pet animals in particular with respect to the problems reported by Customs to fully ensure that only pet animals complying with requirements of Regulation (EC) No 998/2003 or Decision 2007/25/EC enter EU-territory.

To rectify deficiencies noted for the provision of storage rooms at the IC Flight Care 2 at the BIP Brussels-Zaventem and for the maintenance of hygiene in the BIP Oostende airport to comply with the requirements of Directive 97/78/EC and Decision 2001/812/EC.

To rectify the minor shortcoming noted for technical equipment and hygiene at the BIP Brussels-Zaventem and to implement the necessary procedures in the BIPs Gent and Liége to fully comply with the requirements of Directive 97/78/EC and Decision 2001/812/EC.
To provide guidance to BIP staff for consignments of live animals which may need to be send to a quarantine facility under the requirements of Decision 2008/946/EC.

audits.title: Animal welfare - farms and transport

recommendations.text: The Competent Authorities should ensure that the system used to monitor the requirements of Council Directive 2007/43/EC complies fully with all the reporting requirements of Annex V of the Directive and provides satisfactory assurances of the reliability of the information provided to the CA.

The Competent Authorities should take the necessary measures to ensure that, as recommended in FVO report 2009-8255, the situation on farms in Belgium with regard to tail-docking, the provision of suitable manipulable material and implementation of suitable diets for pregnant sows and gilts is improved and brought into full compliance with, respectively, Chapter I, point 8 second paragraph of Annex I, Chapter I, point 4 of Annex I and Article 3(7) of Council Directive 2008/120/EC.

The Competent Authorities should ensure that staff performing approvals and official controls on means of transport approved for long distance receive suitable instructions and guidance as required in Article 8 (1) of Council Regulation (EC) No 882/2004/EC to enable them to effectively assess the records of satellite navigation systems in accordance with Article 15(4) of Council Regulation (EC) No 1/2005 and that mechanical ventilation systems are compliant with the requirements of Points 3(1) and 3(2) of Chapter VI of Annex I of the same Regulation.

The Competent Authorities should take the necessary measures to ensure that certificates of approval issued for means of transport approved for long distance are reviewed and, if necessary, the vehicles are reinspected to ensure that only those complying fully with the requirements of Chapter II and VI of Annex I to Council Regulation (EC) No 1/2005 continue to hold such certificates.

The Competent Authorities should take the necessary measures to address the recommendation from the previous report on checks at unloading in order to comply with Article 3 of Regulation EC (No) 882/2004 which requires controls to be carried out regularly and on a risk basis.

The Competent Authorities should take the necessary measures to improve communication and cooperation with the Police in order to comply with the requirements of Article 4(3) of Regulation EC (No) 882/2004 which provides for efficient and effective co-ordination between Competent Authorities involved in official controls.

The Competent Authorities should take the necessary measures, as recommended in FVO report 2009-8255, to ensure that equipment used for stunning and killing is constructed, maintained and used in such a way as to achieve rapid and effective stunning or killing in accordance with the requirements of Article 6 of Directive 93/119/EC and restraint for ritual slaughter meets the requirements of Annex B (1) of the same Directive.

The Competent Authorities should take the necessary measures, as recommended in FVO report 2009-8255, to ensure that guidance is issued on the strength and duration of current used in waterbath stunners as required by Annex C(II)(3)(B)(1) to Directive93/119/EC.

recommendations.text: ure that the risk based system used for determining the frequency of official controls takes into consideration all provisions of Article 3 (1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 in such a way as to achieve the objectives of this Regulation and that controls over food business operators' compliance with Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005 are carried out with an adequate frequency in all types of establishments as required by the same article of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

responses.response: The system for determining the frequency of official controls in all types of establishments is risk based, also taking into account the feasibility of carrying out these official controls with the available resources and staff. d For the risk ranking of each individual FBO, the presence of a validated own check system, the inspection results and previous sanctions are taken into account. recommendations.text: To improve the system for providing certificates of competence by: · publishing the legislation necessary to approve the training programme, · targeting the animal welfare officer (AWO) training course at the particular operations, species and type of equipment for which each AWO is 18 responsible in their slaughterhouse, and · by setting an examination that provides full assurance of the operator's competence in certain operatio Legal basis for this recommendation: Articles 7(3), 21 and 29(2) of Regulation (EC) No 1099/2009.
recommendations.legal_basis: for this recommendation: Articles 7(3), 21 and 29(2) of Regulation (EC) No 1099/2009.

citations.text: With the transfer of responsibility for animal welfare to the regions, from 1 January 2015 the regions' animal welfare departments are responsible for organising training and exams and awarding certificates of competence for the activities referred to in Article 7(2) of the Regulation, as envisaged by its Article 21.

Pending this change, national level training and exams were organised as follows: · There is a specific university-level course for AWOs. It was noted that all but one of the AWOs met by the audit team had attended this course. As there is not yet legal basis for this course, the CA are not checking that the AWOs have attended this course. · The other slaughterhouse personnel can undergo training organised by a training institute or in-house training organised by the AWO of the slaughterhouse. In the latter case there has to be an independent exam. For this an online exam programme has recently been created which can be accessed from a computer in the slaughterhouse. The exams have to be supervised, and the results validated, by an official veterinarian.

It was noted that certificates awarded to those who take the online exam do not differentiate between tasks. A CCA representative explained that the exam covers all activities as it was difficult to make this differentiation using the on line format used to develop the exam. Exam participants have to respond to pictures rather than plain written questions. On exam questions and topics set in Annex IV to the Regulation, it was noted that when an applicant worked in a slaughterhouse that practiced slaughter without stunning there were no precise questions/pictures regarding this practice, where both the practices and the monitoring of the risks for animal welfare are very different compared to slaughter with stunning. 4

The AWO responsible for one of the slaughterhouses visited that practised slaughter without stunning considered the training material inadequate for the practices in his slaughterhouse. There was no reference to checking for the absence of signs of life which is a key requirement where this type of slaughter is practised. Conclusions on framework for controls

The system for certificates of competence does provide for the required exam with a good emphasis of practical situations through its use of pictures in the assessment. BOs have used the good practice guides effectively, but both these and the exam are not adequately covering tasks in slaughterhouses which present particular risks for animal welfare such as slaughter without stunning.

Publication is expected in September ­ October 2015. - Wallonia: The project will be submitted to the Minister for approval. - Brussels-Capital : The project will be initiated in the Brussels- Capital Region Concerning the training course for animal welfare officers, Belgium already goes beyond the requirements of the Regulation, demanding that this be a course on a university level, while the Regulation only requires a certificate of competence. citations.text: The results of the OVs' official controls were collated in the Foodnet database in such a way that they can be analysed. However, FAFSC has not yet used this data to evaluate and review the system of official checks to ensure that requirements are met and to better prioritise checks on such issues as broiler monitoring, problems reported from checklists and the effectiveness of enforcement in different provinces (see also sections 5.4, 5.5 and 5.6).

Every question on the OV electronic checklist is subject to a weighting factor reflecting the seriousness of non-compliance (see also sections 5.3 and 5.5). 5 · The weighting of the seriousness of non-compliance cases in the checklists triggers action when an individual case of non-compliance scores 10 or when more than 20 % of the items on the checklist are non-compliant. · For example, the lack of signs on lairage pens showing their capacity and the animals' time of arrival scores low in terms of the significance of the non-compliance as there were other ways that the CA checked overnight stays and overstocking.

The checklists for controls are well designed with a weighting factor reflecting the seriousness of non-compliance, however the data produced from the checks is not being adequately used to plan the subsequent controls on the basis of the business operators past records, or to analyse if the weighting factors for the various non- compliances were appropriate.

Centrally, FASFC is not using data such as Foodnet as effectively as it could to ensure requirements are met and to better prioritise checks. In general, analysis of the results of previous checks has not been carried out. In particular, the results of prioritising checks on slaughter without stunning were not available. 6

citations.text: The documented procedures and instructions in place are sufficient for BIP staff to perform the controls correctly and consistently once the consignments are notified. recommendations.text: To ensure that, if the competent authority intends to maintain the initial request, facilities and equipment in the BIP are sufficient and appropriate for each species covered by the approval, as required by Annex A to Council Directive 91/496/EEC.

citations.text: The inspection room is suitable for different species of animals. However, it is not equipped with the necessary tools that would allow staff to perform identity and physical checks (e.g. refrigerator for storing samples, equipment to restrain, equipment to check their identification i.e. microchip readers), contrary to the requirements laid down in Articles 3 and 4 of Decision 97/794/EC.

The existing isolation spaces (kennels) to detain a typical consignment of the species expected are located outside the BIP facilities, near the tarmac. The distance between the kennels and the runaway of the airport is insufficient to mitigate adequately the noise levels. The kennels are not suitable for puppies, small dogs, cats or ferrets: they do not provide lighting, ventilation and/or temperature control. Overall, the isolation facilities proposed cannot ensure that the environmental conditions are adequate to avoid distress to the animals, contrary to the requirements of Regulation (EC) 1/2005.

Contracts and procedures are in place, as required by points 8 and 10 of Annex A to Directive 91/496/EEC, as follows: for cleaning and disinfection of the facilities of the BIP, laboratories where the samples have to be sent, disposal of carcasses/dead animals, and additional veterinary surgeon services. There is no contract for pest control in the area where the kennels are located, outside the building (see finding 16).

The facilities proposed cannot ensure that standards for animal welfare can be maintained for dogs, cats or ferrets, where there is a need for housing. The BIP facilities are adequate for receiving and checking consignments of insects.

citations.text: In the FLVVG-LFSAG (Federal Laboratory for the Safety of the Food Chain Gentbrugge) laboratory visited the audit team saw that a number of honey and hair residue samples were received in the laboratory but two honey and one hair sample went missing before the analysis could be performed. In June 2014 it was reported that this was the second honey sample to go missing in this laboratory in the last eight months. An investigation was performed in the laboratory but the reason for the samples going missing was not identified1. The outcome of the investigation was communicated to DG Laboratories so that further action could be taken (e.g. taking replacement samples).

In two of the slaughterhouses visited, official residue samples were kept in unsecured fridges and freezers, either in storage rooms within the slaughterhouse's own laboratory area or in an unlocked fridge in a room with no access restriction for personnel. The temperature of one freezer was also not monitored. Such unsecured storage is not in line with the requirements of point 2.9 of the Annex to Decision 98/179/EC regarding suitable storage to ensure analyte stability and sample integrity or the requirements of Article 11(7) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 that samples must be handled in such a way as to guarantee both their legal and analytical validity.

Although samples are effectively sealed, such storage does not fully ensure that all samples remain under official control from the time of sampling through to analysis. recommendations.text: To ensure that analytical methods listed in the residue monitoring plan are validated in accordance with Commission Decision 2002/657/EC.

citations.text: The method for quinolones (in operation since 2006) has been validated in accordance with the requirements of Article 3 of Decision 2002/657/EC in bovine muscle. No other muscle matrices (for example pig, poultry, fish and rabbit) have been validated (though there were satisfactory results in proficiency tests for oxolinic acid and difloxacin in rabbit meat in 2009). There are no instructions on how to address possible matrix effects in the general SOP on method validation.

The LC-MS method for sulphonamides in muscle was recently validated at 20 µg/kg (screening) and MRL level (confirmation) in line with the requirements of Article 3 of Decision 2002/657/EC. While the screening method was validated in muscle of different animal species, confirmatory method validation was carried out only in pig muscle samples. No muscle of other animal species (e.g. cattle, fish, and rabbit) was included in the validation study. 9

Notwithstanding shortcomings with regard to verification of method performance in muscle samples of different animal species, the competent authority can have confidence in the reliability of analytical results produced by residue laboratories3.

recommendations.text: To ensure that all treatments applied to food-producing animals are recorded as required in Article 10 of Council Directive 96/23/EC and Annex I, Part A III, point 8(b) to Regulation (EC) No 852/2004.

citations.text: As described in the 2009 FVO report, a special form called document d'administration ou de fourniture (DAF) is used to document veterinary treatments on holdings. Veterinary practitioners are obliged to record on DAFs both medicines personally administered by the veterinarian to animals on the farm during the risk period and those delivered from the veterinary depot to the farmer. The DAF forms seen by the audit team did not include the identification of specific/ individual animals to be treated4. Therefore the DAF form cannot be considered as equivalent to treatment records as required under Article 10 of Directive 96/23/EC and Article 69 of Directive 2001/82/EC. At all three farms visited (cattle, pig, laying hens) these DAF forms were available.

For recording treatments administered to food-producing animals by a farmer, a standardised form (administration/ supply record) is distributed by the Flemish association (Dierengezondheidszorg Vlanderen -DGZ) and the Walloon association (Association Régionale de Santé et d'Identification Animales -ARISA), with the provision that treatment records have to be maintained for each animal species separately (i.e. separate records for cattle, sheep etc.). As recording of withdrawal periods is not foreseen in this form, the content of the form is not fully in line with Article 10 of Directive 96/23/EC and Regulation 852/2004 (Annex I, Part A III, point 8(b))5. Although there is still no legal obligation to register treatments outside the so-called "risk period" (period before animal products are estimated to enter in the food chain, described in the 2009 FVO report), the form was used on cattle and pig farms visited. 4 In their response to the draft report the competent authorities noted that the DAF form includes a column for the identification of the animal or the group of animals treated or for which the medicinal product was supplied and that the column in question has to be filled out by the veterinarian. 5 In their response to the draft report the competent authorities noted that the medicinal products record for farmers does however include a column headed 'N° référence Médicament' [Medicinal product reference No]. This number is that of the DAF or the prescription for the medicine in question, and thanks to this reference it is possible to identify the DAF or the prescription in the IN register and thus to find the withdrawal time. 12

Actions to address the recommendation of the 2009 FVO report to ensure that all treatments applied to food-producing animals are recorded have not been finalised. The competent authority stated that consultations with stakeholders are on-going and that a task force to draft a new legislative act on veterinary medicines records on farms was formed with the target to have the Belgian legislation compliant with EU rules by 1 January 2016. Conclusions

Conditions governing the authorisation and distribution of veterinary medicinal products are in line with EU requirements. recommendations.text: To ensure that food chain information for bovines is implemented in line with the requirements stipulated in Regulation (EC) No 853/2004.

citations.text: Templates for food chain information are in place for all farmed species. However, in the case of cattle, the justification given by the competent authority being a reduction in the administrative burden on farmers, this food chain information has been simplified to a standard declaration on the rear of bovine passports: "Is there pertinent information to mention in the framework of food chain information?" The farmer ticks the box to indicate "yes" or "no" and signs and dates the statement. In the case of ticking "yes" the farmer is given the choice to tick one of two other standard statements: "The information is indicated on the form for this purpose submitted to the slaughterhouse" or "The information has already been transmitted to the slaughterhouse by electronic means".

Such simplified food chain information for bovines is not in line with the requirements of Regulation (EC) No 853/2004, which states in Annex II, Section III that "However, it is not necessary for the slaughterhouse operator to be provided with:....the information referred to in point 3(a), (b), (f) and (g), if the producer 8 In their response to the draft report the competent authorities noted that the frequency depends on the health status of the aquaculture farm and the species kept and is in line with the official minimum inspection frequencies laid down in Directive 2006/88/EC on animal health requirements for aquaculture animals. 14 declares that there is no relevant information to report." This provision does not cover point 3(c) for example: "veterinary medicinal products or other treatments, administered to the animals within a relevant period and with a withdrawal period greater than zero, together with their dates of administration and withdrawal periods."

The system in place for controls on the distribution and use of veterinary medicinal products is well designed, notwithstanding the fact that the simplified food chain information introduced for bovines in the form of a farmer declaration is not in line with EU requirements and weakens the effectiveness of said system as regards investigations of non-compliant results. As regards equidae, the system for the identification of horses is in place and controls on slaughtered horses are being effectively implemented.

audits.title: Plant Health - Import Controls

recommendations.text: Ensure that import checks and, in particular, plant health checks are based on a representative sample as required by Article 13a(1)(b)(iii) of Directive 2000/29/EC.

citations.text: The manual on phytosanitary import control has an attachment with 12 sampling tables for visual inspection for different types of commodities prepared on the basis of ISPM 31. These tables define the number of units for sampling e.g. fruits, sachets, bunches of flowers, to be selected for visual inspection. For each type of commodity, a sampling matrix at confidence level of 95% and 99% is set as per ISPM 31. In addition for each confidence level, two columns with sampling sizes for different detection levels varying from 1% to 5% are set. The sampling size i.e. the column to be used depends on the level of risk established for the lot or consignment. Default sampling rate for all types of commodities is low risk. However, the sampling size for large consignments which are qualified as low risk of fruit and vegetables was considered by the FVO team as not appropriate e.g. 60 pieces of fruit for a large consignment.

The FVO team witnessed plant health checks of fruit (pomelo and lime), vegetables (green chillies and bitter gourd) and cut flowers (gypsophila) and noted that: Inspectors had appropriate technical competence regarding the detection of HOs in commodities which they regularly inspected; Inspections witnessed were meticulous. Inspectors checking cut flowers were shaking bunches above a paper sheet for the detection of thrips. All the bunches were opened for additional examination of the leaves under the illuminated magnifying lens; The inspection of fruit consisted of random selection of the required number of fruit from different boxes to meticulously inspect them with a magnifying glass. 10% of fruits selected for visual inspection were peeled and cut to check for the presence of any larvae; For the inspection of vegetables, 10 boxes were selected and from each box 15 fruits were taken for visual examination as they determined as a high risk commodity. After visual inspection of the sample some suspicious fruits were brought to the BIP office for detailed examination under the binocular microscope. A thrip was detected there and a sample was taken for determination in the laboratory; Inspections were carried out in adequate conditions of lighting; The size of the sample taken for visual inspection was always in line with the FASFC guidelines.

The definition of the "unit" to be sampled for visual inspection in the FASFC guidelines is not appropriate for some commodities e.g. a single fruit of small green chilli counts as a unit. For a large consignment of chillies the sampling size would be 60 pieces for low risk or 150 pieces for high risk consignment. The sample size inspected for large consignments of fruit and vegetables is not in line with ISPM 31 and cannot be considered as a representative sample. This does not comply with Article 13a(1)(b)(iii) of Directive 2000/29/EC. In view of ISPM 31, the sample size should be big enough to result in a satisfactorily probability for finding pests. 13

Plant health checks are carried out meticulously, however the quantity of units inspected for some commodities is significantly below the recommended quantity and cannot be considered as representative. Therefore, recommendation (6) of the previous report has not been fully addressed.

responses.response: instructions in relation to the sampling units for fruit and vegetables will be adapted by 30/06/2016.

citations.text: There is not a procedure in place for monitoring of non-regulated products. They are checked only if presented in mixed consignments, in consignments of fruits and vegetables which are subject to marketing standards quality controls and in consignments of non-animal origin in case of suspicion of the presence of HOs. audits.title: National Audit Systems

recommendations.text: The competent authorities responsible for controls on animal welfare should ensure that adequate audit arrangements are put in place to achieve the objectives of Article 4(6) of regulation (EC) No. 882/2004 and that appropriate measures are taken in the light of the results of those audits.

citations.text: In 2014, responsibility for animal welfare was transferred from federal level to the three Belgian Regions (Flanders, Wallonia and Brussels Capital). At the time of the DG SANTE audit, protocols had been signed between FASFC and each of the Regions under which FASFC will perform animal welfare controls at slaughterhouses and on farms. Regions remain directly responsible for follow-up of non-compliance and any necessary enforcement action arising from the results of the controls carried out by FASFC. The management contracts defining the modalities of the controls were in the course of being finalised and signed. The IAU informed the DG SANTE audit team that the contracts include a provision for the Regions to audit, or have audits carried out on, the animal welfare controls performed by FASFC on their behalf. 5.1.2.2 Responsibility for audits of official controls

The DG SANTE audit team met with representatives from the Regions, responsible for controls on animal welfare. A representative of the regional internal audit service of the Flanders Region was also present. In the case of Flanders, the internal audit representative confirmed that his service was aware of the need to plan audits in relation to animal welfare controls to meet the requirements of Article 4(6) of Regulation (EC) No. 882/2004 and that while the planning for 2016 did not include its topic, audits were expected to take place in 2018. The modalities of these audits had not been confirmed. At the time of the DG SANTE audit, the representatives of the Walloon and Brussels Capital Regions could not confirm what audit arrangements would be put in place. Conclusions

Responsibility for auditing of official controls has also been clearly allocated, with the exception of controls on animal welfare falling under the scope of Regulation (EC) No. 882/2004, for which auditing arrangements have not yet been defined.

audits.title: Organic Farming

recommendations.text: Ensure that provisions in regional legislation as well as their implementation are in line with relevant provisions of the EU organic regulations, in particular with regard to The mutilation of animals (Article 18 of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008) The shortening of conversion period (Article 36(2)(b) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008) The grazing of animals (Article 14(2)(b)(ii) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007 and Article 14(2) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008) The tethering of animals in small holdings (Article 39 of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008) The controls of retailers (Article 27(3) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007)

citations.text: Some requirements in the regional legislations and / or their implementation are not in line with EU rules. This mainly relates to exceptional production rules (see chapter 5.2.7), conditions for the grazing of cattle (paragraph 40) as well as the exemption and control of retailers (see paragraph 27 and 30). Conclusions on National Legislation and Provisions

Regional provisions are in place to implement legally binding Union acts. However, some of these provisions and / or their implementation are not in line with requirements of the EU organic regulations.

All three Regions made use of Article 28(2) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007 and exempted retailers selling pre-packed products to the final consumer. According to Article 4.2 and 4.3 of the Decree of Wallonia and Article 4.2 and 4.3 of the Decree of Bruxelles-Capital the exemption from official controls is limited to retailers with an annual turnover of less than 5,000 Euros (of sales of organic products) in these two Regions provided conditions laid down in Article 28(2) of the above mentioned regulation are fulfilled.However, CAs confirmed that no controls are undertaken to verify whether exempted retailers fulfil conditions for exemption from official controls provided for in Article 28(2) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. Conclusions on Registration of Operators

The system in place generally ensures that operators are registered and that key information about their organic activity is made publicly accessible by CAs. However, there is no system in place to verify whether exempted retailers fulfil conditions for 6 exemption. Moreover, documentary evidences issued by CB do not necessarily follow the model provided for in the EU regulation. 5.2.3 Planning and Prioritisation of Controls Legal Requirements Articles 3 and 41 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 Article 27(3) and 28(2) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007 Articles 65(4) and 92c(2) of Commission Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 Findings

All operators certified by the CBs visited receive at least one annual control. However, Article 17 of the Decree of the Flemish Government referred to in paragraph 2 provides for partial annual checks on retailers provided that controls cover all aspects during a period of three years. This is not in line with Article 27(3) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007 which requires that operators, with the exception of wholesalers and operators selling to the final consumer or user as described in Article 28(2) of the same regulation, must be subject to a verification of compliance once a year.

CBs' control plans are based on an assessment of the risk which is generally adequate and efforts are made to increase the effectiveness of controls by improving the planning of visits to processors. CBs conduct a high number of controls which potentially compensate the risk related to the fact that not all CBs directly consider production quantities in their risk evaluation of operators. Some key information is not yet reported in the framework of the MANCP. 5.2.4 Controls of operators Legal Requirements Articles 8 and 9 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 Titles II and III of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007 Title II and IV of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 Article 65 of Commission Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 Findings

At a dairy farm, the audit team noted that the CB accepts that operators may keep animals permanently indoors up to an age of six months, even during the grazing period. The responsible CA confirmed that the CB follows relevant instructions adopted by the advisory committee referred to in paragraph 22. This is not in line with Article 14(2)(b)(ii) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007 and Article 14(2) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 which stipulates that herbivores shall have access to pastures for grazing whenever conditions allow. Conclusions on Controls at Operators

Controls at operators were overall effective although some shortcomings were observed with regard to the control of labelling of organic products, the calculation of input/output and the records of the verification of the organic status of products when received by operators. The implementation of some production rules is not in line with EU organic regulation. 5.2.5 Controls on Labelling and Traceability Legal Requirements Article 23 and 24 of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007 Title III of Commission Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 9 Findings

As regards dehorning of animals, derogations granted by CAs to individual operators are valid for one year and for an estimated number of animals. In the case of CB1 applications by farmers are accepted before animals are born. This is not in line with 11 Article 18 of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 which does not provide for routine dehorning, but requires a case-by-case assessment before derogation can be granted. The CB assesses the case and forwards a proposal for decision to the CA. However, no documents are provided to the CA to support the CB proposal.

CB1 stated that dehorning has to be done within seven days of birth of the animal. In the case of CB2, the audit team noted that derogations were granted for the dehorning of animals of up to 6 months of age and more. During inspections observed, it was not verified whether animals when dehorned were of appropriate age and subject to application of appropriate anaesthesia/analgesia as required by Article 18(2) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008.

During witness audits, it was noted that a conversion period of three months was granted to an operator who produces vegetables in glasshouses. The CB stated that it followed relevant instructions provided by the CA (Flanders) on its website. This was confirmed by the relevant CA. The CA further stated that pesticides which were not authorised for organic production were previously used on production in hydroculture and that the soil, at that time, was covered with plastic film which prevented contamination. This was confirmed by a soil sample (no residues) before the three months conversion period was granted to the operator. This is not in line with Article 36(2)(b) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 which stipulates that the parcels for which the conversion period is reduced were natural or agricultural areas which were not treated with non-authorised products over a period of three years before such derogation can be granted.

Regional legislations (see paragraph 2) allow for the tethering of animals in holdings having less than 50 animals. However, no evidence was provided to the audit team demonstrating that all other specific conditions laid down in Article 39 of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 are verified by CAs before the derogation is granted. Conclusions on Exceptional Production Rules and Other Derogations

Some of the regional provisions for exceptional production rules and other derogations, as well as their implementation, are not in line with EU rules. 5.2.8 Imports of Products from Organic Production Legal Requirements Articles 32 and 33 of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007 Chapter 3 of Title III and Annexes II, III, V and VI of Commission Regulation (EC) No 1235/2008 Findings

responses.response: The regional legislations will be adjusted where needed: The mutilation of animals: the recognised control bodies will be reminded that in accordance with the provisions of Art. 18 of Reg. 889/2008 any suffering to the animals shall be reduced to a minimum by carrying out the operation only at the most appropriate age. The requirements on the applications, granting and control of mutilation of animals will be reinforced The shortening of conversion period: BE is of the opinion that the requirements regarding the shortening of the conversion period are implemented correctly. The grazing of animals: (i) the reference to Article 14(2)(b)(ii) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007 is invalid (ii) in accordance with Article 14(1)(b)(ii) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007 "husbandry practices, including [...] housing conditions shall ensure that the developmental, physiological and ethological needs of animals are met"; BE considers the latter article must be taken into account when deciding whether or not it is found appropriate to keep calves under six months inside the buildings. Tethering of animals: BE is of the opinion that the requirements regarding the tethering of animals in small holdings

recommendations.text: Ensure that, in line with Article 27(1) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007, the control system set up in Belgium duly provides for the designation of CAs responsible for controls in respect to all obligations established in the EU organic regulations, and in particular with regard to import controls, including those relating to electronic certification, as laid down in Regulation (EC) No 1235/2008.

citations.text: Customs is responsible for general import controls. There is however no CA responsible for import controls of organic goods and the implementation of relevant EU requirements. This is not in line with Article 27(1) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007 which requires EU MSs to designate one or more competent authorities responsible for controls in respect of the obligations established in the EU organic regulations (see also chapter 5.2.8)

The regional CAs stated that a protocol is being developed between the Regions and Customs for the implementation of the electronic certification via the Trade Control and Expert System New Technology (TRACES NT) applicable as of October 2017. However, neither a draft nor a deadline for finalization of such a document could be provided by the regional CAs or Customs to the audit team. This, together with the fact that no CA is currently responsible for import controls, puts at risk the timely implementation of the electronic certification system.

Files reviewed confirmed that good communication is in place between the regional CAs and the paying agencies concerning irregularities relating to EU organic rules and the exchange of other relevant information such as the list of land parcels managed by an organic farmer. However, irregularities related to imported goods are not shared in a systematic manner by the regional CAs with Customs (see paragraph 62). Conclusions Competent Authorities and Control Bodies

The control system for organic production is only partially in place. Although competencies and related obligations are well defined at regional level, no CA is responsible for import controls of organic goods (see also chapter 5.2.8). 5.2.1.1 Control Bodies: Approval, Supervision and Withdrawal 4 Legal Requirements Articles 5(2) and (3) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 Articles 27(5) to (9) and 27(14) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007 Articles 92c and 92e of Commission Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 Findings
There is no CA designed for import controls of organic products in Belgium, contrary to Article 27(1) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. 12

Provisions of Regulation (EC) No 1235/2008 in relation to the EU import of organic products such as the risk assessment to determine the frequency of physical checks or the sampling of consignments of organic products before they are released for free circulation into the EU by Customs are not implemented.

Customs may receive, on an ad-hoc basis, information from regional CAs as regards organic consignments entering into the EU via Belgium. The audit team was presented some examples showing that organic consignments from Ukraine, Russia and Kazakhstan were sampled. However, the CAs could neither present an overview nor could they provide evidence to confirm that all organic consignments from Ukraine, Russia and Kazakhstan had been subject to the reinforced control measures adopted by the EU.

In a case reviewed by the audit team, an organic consignment was imported into Belgium without a Certificate of Inspection. This was discovered by the CB during control at the importer who had imported this consignment. The CB notified the regional CA, but the irregularity was not shared with Customs. Conclusions on Imports of Products from Organic Productions

Import controls may take place on an ad-hoc basis in Belgium. However there is no CA responsible for import controls and it is currently not ensured that relevant control requirements are implemented. 5.2.9 Measures in cases of irregularities and infringements Legal Requirements Articles 54, 55(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 Article 27(5)(d) and 30 of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007 Articles 91, 92, 92(a) and (d) of Commission Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 Findings
