citations.text: A calculation of the balance of input and output was conducted during all inspections observed. The exercise was mainly based on documentary checks and often did not include the verification of the real situation on the spot. At the egg producers visited, the input/output calculation focused on feed consumption per hen per day for a randomly selected hen house. The data related to an appropriate period, starting from the stocking day of the house with hens up to the inspection day. Inspectors took data from records such as the volume of feed in stock, but did not verify the real amount of the feed still in stock on the day of inspection. At a plant producer, the inspector verified invoices for sale but did not check plausibility of these quantities by comparing them with actual production data and estimated yields. At one of the processors visited, the inspector did not verify the accuracy of the records kept by the operator regarding quantities produced and sold, despite the fact that relevant invoices were available. This is not in line with Article 66 of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 which requires that documentary accounts are used to verification operations performed by the operator.

At one of the processors visited, the internal checklist for reception of goods referred to food safety aspects only but not to verification of the organic status of a product. This had never been raised as non-compliant by the CBs in the past. The CBs visited confirmed that operators are not required to record the verification of the organic status of the goods at reception which is not in line with Article 66(2) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008.

Controls at operators were overall effective although some shortcomings were observed with regard to the control of labelling of organic products, the calculation of input/output and the records of the verification of the organic status of products when received by operators. The implementation of some production rules is not in line with EU organic regulation. 5.2.5 Controls on Labelling and Traceability Legal Requirements Article 23 and 24 of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007 Title III of Commission Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 9 Findings

As regards the labelling, a number of labels on packaging of organic products were seen which included a reference to both, EU and non-EU agriculture, on the same label despite the fact that ingredients were of either EU or non-EU origin. The CAs stated that such reference, i.e. EU / non-EU on the same package, is considered acceptable mainly for practical reason, even if this reference does not always fully reflect the content of the product. This is not in line Article 24(1)(c) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. At another operator certified by CB1, the size of the EU logo on the label used did not meet the minimum dimensions set out in point 7 of Annex XI of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. The labels were provided by the operator's producer association who market the operator's production to final consumers. The producer association is also certified by CB1. This issue has never been raised as non-compliant by the CB either during the inspection observed by the audit team or during previous inspections. At another operator (CB2), the packaging material used for the processed product did not show the CB code number as required by Article 24(1)(a) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. The CB has never requested the correction of this non-compliance although the operator has been using this type of packing material for several years. Conclusions on Labelling and Traceability

The system in place generally allows for traceability of organic products at all stages. However, controls of labels were superficial and the lack of obligatory information was overlooked with the risk that consumers are misled or that key information to ensure traceability of a product is not provided. 5.2.6 Sampling and laboratory analysis Legal Requirements Article 12 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 Article 65 (2) of Commission Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 Findings

recommendations.text: Ensure that laboratories used by CBs for the testing of organic samples are designated by CAs as required by Article 12(2) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

citations.text: The two CBs visited have a list of laboratories which are used for the testing of organic samples. These laboratories are accredited to ISO 17025, but they are not designated by the CAs for the testing of organic products as required by Article 12(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

The CAs of Flanders and Wallonia stated that the scope of active substances tested by the laboratories in the case of organic samples is verified during supervision of CBs. However, the audit team noted that result of such verification was not reported by the CAs in the relevant supervisory reports.

The CBs visited, stated that, in relation to the scope of active substances analysed for, they relied on the fact that the laboratory was accredited. In their view, accreditation implied that the laboratory would be aware of the appropriate testing scope for organic samples. Nevertheless evidence was seen that CBs request single residue methods when required, for example when substances such as glyphosate have to be tested for.

The high number of samples annually taken by the CBs is based on an adequate risk assessment and laboratories used by CBs are accredited. However, laboratories are not designated by the CA as required by EU legislation. 5.2.7 Exceptional production rules and other derogations. Legal Requirements Article 29 and sections 2 to 4 of Chapter 6 of Title II of Commission Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 Findings

responses.response: he Regional Competent authorities will explore the opportunities arding the designation of laboratories. In a first stage, the laboratories designated by de federal food safety agency will be taken into account. recommendations.text: Ensure that enforcement measures imposed by CBs in particular in case of sever and recurrent non-compliances are sufficiently effective to ensure compliance with Article 30 of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. 19

citations.text: The catalogues of measures are overall comprehensive and the files reviewed by the audit team confirmed that the CBs apply measures in line with the catalogues. However, 13 the majority of measures provided for in these catalogues consist only of light action such as "observation", "comment", "warning", "a request for improvement" and enhanced controls". Moreover, operators who use conventional seeds without prior approval receive a "warning" in Flanders and a "request for improvement" in Wallonia.

Files reviewed and inspections observed during the audit confirmed that measures imposed by CBs in particular in cases of severe and/or recurrent non-compliances were not sufficiently effective to ensure compliance with Article 30 of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007: An organic operator was only issued a "request for improvement" for the recurrent use of conventional seed without prior-derogation from the CB. The field in question was only declassified after the operator was found to have used conventional seeds without prior-approval for the fifth time. The inspection history of an operator visited showed recurrent non-compliances such as insufficient separation, incorrect calculation of the balance of input/output for several organic products, lack of notification of new products to the CB and the selling of several products labelled organic without certification. Despite these severe non-compliances with organic rules, the CB continued to certify the operator. Similar non-compliances were detected during the witness audit and the CB decided to suspend the certificate following this visit. In several cases, it was noted by the audit team that the CBs continued certifying operators before non-compliances with production rules, such as excessive stocking density, inadequate area for animals were corrected by the operators and verified by the CB. Moreover, the CBs visited confirmed that an irregularity noted at an operator is disregarded after a period of 24 months elapses and that, if then the same irregularity occurs, the softest measures suggested in the sanction catalogues would be applied.

The CBs visited apply a "soft" approach with regard to enforcement measures in particular in cases of severe and recurrent irregularities. This, together with the fact that not all irregularities are either reported to relevant CAs or fully investigated by CBs, reduces the effectiveness of the control system.

responses.response: gium was one of the first Member States to dispose of a national legally binding catalogue of measures. This catalogue has proven to be useful for years. Nevertheless Belgium acknowledges that there is room for improvement. We will take into account as much as possible the experiences and examples of good practices from other Member States (a project which is encouraged by the organic unit from DG AGRI) to improve our catalogue of measures. In accordance with the regional regulations, reviewing the catalogue of sanctions must be carried out in consultation with the sector, through discussion in the framework of the advisory committees. Taking account of the procedural steps to be followed and of the sensitivity of the issue at stake, BE foresees to adopt the necessary legal bases in 2019.

recommendations.text: Ensure that CBs take appropriate measures in case of suspicion of irregularities and do not put products on the market until they satisfy themselves that the doubt has been eliminated in line with Article 91 of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008.

citations.text: Regional legislations require the investigation of irregularities irrespective of the level of residues of non-authorised products / pesticides found in an organic product.
However, files reviewed by the audit team confirmed that not all such cases were investigated in line with Article 91 of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008.

CB2 confirmed that in cases where samples taken from raw material not yet used by a processor show residues below the limit referred to above, the processor can use the material in question, as the processor in question is not guilty of the contamination, which must have occurred earlier in the food chain. The CB stated that it would not await the outcome of the investigation contrary to Article 91 of the above mentioned regulation. Moreover, the CB confirmed that the producer of the raw material would not necessarily be informed of the incidence, which is not in line with Article 92(4) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 requiring the CB to inform without delay the CB of the operator who had produced the product in question.

In another case, CB2 had taken two samples from a batch in order to investigate a 14 suspicion notified by the importer of the product (Cumin) in question. The CB sent one of the two samples taken to the laboratory. The sample tested positive for cypermethrin (0.015 mg/kg). The operator required the counter sample to be tested which did not show any residue of the insecticide. The CB accepted the result from the counter sample and the product was sold as organic. However, the audit team noted that 1) the counter sample was tested in a laboratory which was chosen by the operator but was not listed in the CB procedures and 2) that the sample taken by the operator prior to the sampling by the CB also contained residues of cypermethrin. The CB was aware of this and confirmed that, in cases where a counter sample has to be tested, the operator has the possibility to choose the laboratory. The CB also confirmed that in the case of contradictory laboratory results, the result of the counter sample would always overrule the result of the first sample and that such cases would not be further investigated to verify whether the operator had complied with the organic rules. This is not in line with Article 91 of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 which requires that the product cannot be placed on the market with indications referring to the organic production method until it is satisfied, on the basis of the information received from the operator or from other sources, that the doubt has been eliminated.

The CBs visited apply a "soft" approach with regard to enforcement measures in particular in cases of severe and recurrent irregularities. This, together with the fact that not all irregularities are either reported to relevant CAs or fully investigated by CBs, reduces the effectiveness of the control system.

recommendations.text: Ensure that irregularities and the likelihood of irregularities are communicated by CBs to CAs, in line with Article 27(5)(e) and Article 30 of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007 as well as Article 92(4) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008, respectively.

citations.text: Files reviewed during the audit confirmed that, in line with regional requirements, CBs communicated to the regional CAs the lists of all operators on a monthly basis as well as 5 enforcement measures imposed by CBs twice per year. However, shortcomings have been identified with regard to the communication of irregularities and the likelihood of irregularities by CBs to the CAs (see chapter 5.2.9). Conclusions on Control Bodies: Approval, Supervision and Withdrawal

Supervision of CBs by regional CAs is only partially implemented. Good coordination and communication is in place with regard to certain aspects, although there are shortcomings regarding the communication of irregularities by CBs to the CAs (see also chapter 5.2.9). 5.2.2 Registration of operators Legal Requirements Article 28(1), (2) and (5) of Council Regulation (EC) No 834/2007 Article 92b of Commission Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 Findings

CB2 confirmed that in cases where samples taken from raw material not yet used by a processor show residues below the limit referred to above, the processor can use the material in question, as the processor in question is not guilty of the contamination, which must have occurred earlier in the food chain. The CB stated that it would not await the outcome of the investigation contrary to Article 91 of the above mentioned regulation. Moreover, the CB confirmed that the producer of the raw material would not necessarily be informed of the incidence, which is not in line with Article 92(4) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 requiring the CB to inform without delay the CB of the operator who had produced the product in question.

Regional legislations require immediate notification of irregularities in cases (i) which involve operators controlled/certified by other CBs, and (ii) when products, plots, or operators are to be decertified by CAs. In Flanders, such notifications have to be done within three working days. In the other two regions, no deadline is imposed, which means that immediate notification is required according to the understanding of the two CAs concerned.

Both CBs confirmed that CAs are formally notified when irregularities involve operators in non-EU countries. This is not in line with Article 92(4) of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008 which requires that CBs, when identifying irregularities with regard to products under the control of other control bodies, shall inform those control bodies without delay. Nevertheless, CBs copy, on an ad-hoc basis, CAs into email communication by which operators are informed of irregularities. Moreover, CBs confirmed that the likelihood of irregularities are not required to be notified to CAs, which is not in line with Article 27(5)(d) of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007.

Files reviewed by the audit team confirmed that findings of residues of non-authorised pesticides below the limit established in the regional legislations are not notified by the CBs to the relevant CAs. Moreover, CB2 did not notify cases of samples which showed multiple residues of non-authorised pesticides, neither was a case notified to the CA where a feed sample showed pesticide residues beyond the above mentioned limit. The 15 CB stated the case was not notified because no feed was left to be decertified. Conclusions on Measures in case of Irregularities and Infringements

The CBs visited apply a "soft" approach with regard to enforcement measures in particular in cases of severe and recurrent irregularities. This, together with the fact that not all irregularities are either reported to relevant CAs or fully investigated by CBs, reduces the effectiveness of the control system.

recommendations.text: To ensure, that microbiological sampling and record keeping of the 30 days validation of processing method 7 is in line as required by point G, Chapter III, Annex IV of Regulation (EU) No 142/2011.

citations.text: All Category 3 processing plants visited were using processing method 7 which had been validated by the ABP operators and authorised by the OVAM. All analytical reports of the samples taken during the 30 days period of validation required by Article 8 and point G(1), Chapter III of Annex IV to Commission Regulation (EU) No 142/2011 were available. In one plant several cases were found by the audit team where samples for detection of Clostridium perfringens had not been taken directly after the treatment. This is not in line with the requirements of point G1(c)(i), Chapter III, Annex IV of Regulation (EU) No 142/2011. The audit team noted that in two of the three processing plants visited records of temperatures (which is a critical control point) used during the validation period were not available. The inspector explained that temperature diagrams were checked during the validation on the screen of the computer and that these records were not saved/maintained. This is not fully in line with the requirements of point G2, Chapter III, Annex IV of Regulation (EU) No 142/2011.2

Shortcomings in record keeping and sampling in relation to official verification of operators` validation of processing method 7 questions the reliability of method performance.

recommendations.text: To ensure that the departure of consignments of processed animal protein is notified in TRACES as required by Article 48(3) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009.

citations.text: The FASFC prepared a service note on the requirements of intra-union trade of PAP and MBM. The note which is applicable only to staff working under the responsibility of FASFC, contains a comprehensive description of the obligation of the Belgian competent authority to notify the competent authority of destination about the departure of the consignments and also on the obligation to notify the competent authority of origin about the arrival of the consignments through the TRAde Control and Expert System (TRACES), as required by Article 48 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009..

Although official controls on ABPs and derived products fall under the responsibility of several Federal and/or Regional competent authorities, the system is well designed and the controls which are risk-based are underpinned by comprehensive establishment listing, well-managed cooperation and communication within and between the different Federal and Regional authorities and, with the exception of the use of TRACES, comprehensive instructions and guidance for inspectors. Shortcomings in record keeping and sampling in relation to official verification of operators` validation of processing method 7 questions the reliability of method performance.

The audit team visited a storage plant which imported PAP from third countries. The company had a well-designed storage system to avoid mixing the PAP of different batches. The company traceability system was also clear and well-managed. The imported products were accompanied by a health certificate and the TRACES document. Some parts of the imported PAP were transported to other Member States for pet food production, but TRACES documents were never issued for these transports, which is not in line with the requirements of article 48 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009. The local inspector did not identify the lack of TRACES notifications during the official controls. 11

Nevertheless, checks on the implementation of requirements concerning preparation and confirmation of TRACES notifications of intra-Union trade of PAP and OF/SI are not adequate. This weakness partly undermines the reliability of the flow of information of the intra EU-trade of such products.

responses.response: A specific question to verify the required TRACES messages have en send by the operator will be taken up in the checklist of the FASFC for storage plants for derived products (including PAP), during the next revision. The concerned sector organizations will be reminded on these requirements during the next available platform of the Feed and ABP sector.

Shortcomings in record keeping and sampling in relation to official verification of operators` validation of processing method 7 questions the reliability of method performance.

The audit team noted that, although training and instructions were provided (see findings 5 and 19), in several cases, arrivals of consignments of PAP were not confirmed by the Belgian competent authorities to the competent authorities of the Member State of origin through TRACES, contrary to Article 48(3) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009. In 2017 around 25% of such arrivals were not notified and this increased to 60% in 2018.3

recommendations.text: To ensure that the departure of consignments of organic fertilisers and soil improvers containing PAP is notified in TRACES as required by Article 48(3) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009.

citations.text: The FASFC issued a circular letter relating to OF/SI containing PAP and/or MBM. The letter contained detailed information about the necessity of TRACES notification. If the OF/SI is going to intra-Union trade, TRACES notification is only necessary if it is pure (100%) PAP and/or MBM. This is not fully in line with the requirement of Article 48 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009. The FASFC stated, that export of OF/SI with ruminant PAP is not allowed according to national legislation. Based on chapter 5 of the farm control checklist, if OF/SI were used in the 21 days prior to the date of the control, the inspector has to check on-the-spot that the exact parcel of land - where the OF/SI was used - fulfils the legal requirements of Chapter II, Annex XI of Regulation (EU) No 142/2011 (see finding 29). Such controls are carried out generally every 8 years.

Although official controls on ABPs and derived products fall under the responsibility of several Federal and/or Regional competent authorities, the system is well designed and the controls which are risk-based are underpinned by comprehensive establishment listing, well-managed cooperation and communication within and between the different Federal and Regional authorities and, with the exception of the use of TRACES, comprehensive instructions and guidance for inspectors. Shortcomings in record keeping and sampling in relation to official verification of operators` validation of processing method 7 questions the reliability of method performance.

One OF/SI manufacturer visited produced OF/SI from PAP and MBM. The commercial packaging of these products was small bags (less than 50kg) and big bags (less than 1000 kg). The company exported only small bags to third countries which contain PAP from non-ruminant and the concentration is up to 75%. The company traded with other Member States small bags containing up to 90% of MBM and big bags containing up to 50% of PAP and/or MBM. There were no TRACES notifications relating to these consignments (see finding 23). Belgium did not use the possibility described in point 3, 10 Section 1, Chapter II, Annex XI of Regulation (EU) No 142/2011 to authorise a component which makes big bags of OF/SI unpalatable. The competent authority stated that the guarantees requested by national legislation fulfil the requirements of point 4(b) Section 1, Chapter II, Annex XI of Regulation (EU) No 142/2011. These guarantees are: big bags are labelled with the obligatory labelling requirements described in point 2(b)(xi), Chapter II, Annex VIII of Regulation (EU) No 142/2011, additional labelling requirements such as "not destined for land to which farmed animals have access, store in place physically separated from livestock", sealing at the top and the bottom of the big bags, regular official controls on farms using OF/SI (see finding 23).

The audit team noted that, as a general policy in Belgium, intra-Union trade of consignments OF/SI containing not pure (100%) PAP and/or MBM (see findings 23) are not notified in TRACES, contrary to Article 48(3) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009. This was confirmed during visit of an OF/SI manufacturer (see finding 29). 5.2.3 Exports and imports of PAP

recommendations.text: To ensure that the seals of exported consignments of processed animal protein are checked at the point of exit from the EU, that the records of these checks are recorded in TRACES and that the competent authority responsible for the processing plant from which the consignment originated verifies that the seal checks have been carried out, as required by points 1(c)(d), Section E, Chapter V, Annex IV of Regulation (EC) No 999/2001.

citations.text: The FASFC prepared a comprehensive procedure on export of PAP-containing ruminant protein. The procedure provides detailed instructions on the control of seals at the BIP. There are also detailed instructions on recording the outcome of the control in TRACES (fulfil relevant parts of the control page). The audit team found that there was no instruction on the obligation for the competent authority responsible for the establishment of origin to carry out regular controls to verify the correct application of seals and verify that confirmation from the point of exit on the identity (seal) control, had been received through TRACES. Such confirmation is required by point 1.(d), Section E, Chapter V, Annex IV of Regulation (EC) No 999/2001.

In one processing plant visited in 2018 (up until the end of August), 467 consignments of PAP containing ruminant protein were sent to third countries (the total number of export consignments containing ruminant PAP from Belgium in that period was 2100). In 2018, the point of exit was different on the transport documents and TRACES documents in around 30 cases (e.g. transport document Antwerp and Rotterdam, TRACES only Antwerp). The representative of the BIP mentioned in the TRACES document confirmed that these consignments had never arrived at the point of exit. audits.title: Food improvement agents

recommendations.text: The control measures foreseen should be put in place in order to ensure adequate coverage of Food Improvement Agent legislation during official controls.

citations.text: The current control system in place does not compel control staff to check, during inspections at FBOs whether the use of FIAs in foodstuffs fully complies with the relevant EU legislation. The pool of inspectors that should carry out second line inspections, is not in place yet7.

There is a system in place for the official controls of FIAs, including import, marketing and their use that is overall fit for purpose, and includes appropriate action in case of non-compliance. However, checks of compliance with the FIAs legislation are only carried out now and then since 2016, at the initiative of individual inspectors. Therefore the production, marketing and use of FIAs are not systematically subject to verification and enforcement where necessary, as regards the FIAs legislation. 8

audits.title: Horse meat

recommendations.text: To take further measures aimed at verifying that owners/keepers of horses 2. meet the obligations of Articles 11, 12, 27 and 35 of Regulation (EU) 2015/262 and, mainly, concerning timely identification, the notification of animals which are permanently brought in Belgium from another countries, the change in their status (from food producing animals to animals which are excluded from slaughter for human consumption), and/or the death of the animals, in order to provide reasonable assurance that the information contained in the CED is up-to-date and reflects the status of the horses kept in the country. To take measures aimed at verifying that, when horses eligible for slaughter for human consumption are treated with medicinal products, the obligations laid down in Article 37 of Regulation (EU) 2015/262 concerning the medication records in the passport and the transmission of relevant information to the PIB and/or to the CED are met; in particular: - in case of non-permitted treatments, the exclusion of the animal from the food chain should be recorded and the information transmitted to the relevant authorities and/or PIB; - when permitted treatments are given (Article 37(6) of Regulation (EU) 2015/262), they are properly registered in the relevant section of the passport. To ensure that when carcases of death animals are disposed or processed in rendering plants, there are measures in place to protect the transponder from subsequent fraudulent use as required by Article 34 of Regulation (EU) 2015/262. In particular, the system in place should provide guarantees that the transponder code implanted on the animal corresponds with the transponder code destroyed or disposed.

citations.text: The CCA and CAs met explained that although there are legal bases and procedures in place for applying sanctions, it is sometimes challenging to enforce the requirements of the legislation in the sector audited, mainly due to difficulties in carrying out official controls for detecting certain non-compliances and for gathering the evidence to support them. For instance, it is their view that the following obligations are difficult to enforce: The verification of the registration of medical treatments in the passports by the treating veterinarian including the activities of the private veterinarian. 8 The verification that the change of keeper is communicated by the new keeper to CBC for registration; Verification of passports issued in other countries and the status of these horses in the central horses databases from the issuing countries, due to legibility issues (see also paragraphs 58, 61 and 79.a); Ensuring that the information flow requirements of Articles 34 and 35 of Regulation (EU) 2015/262 are complied with after the death of an equine animal, in the case of fallen stock, and that the corresponding passports are rendered invalid and are sent to the PIBs (see paragraph 88.b). Notification of the movement of horses leaving the territory or notification of the death of an animal (see also paragraph 63). Coordination and collaboration between CAs, PIBs and sport associations

The audit team noted the following concerning the procedure for the handling of passports and the transmission of the data to the CED: a. The passports of slaughtered animals were invalidated and returned to the CBC offices. In one slaughterhouse visited, the CED was updated on-line, whereas in the other slaughterhouse the passport was not always returned within the specified deadlines (5 working days after slaughter); the stamp used in one slaughterhouse did not explicitly invalidate the passports. b. The rendering company visited ­ the only such facility in Belgium - omits to read, record and transmit the number of transponders from fallen stock they collect to the CED, which is not in compliance with the Art. 44.1 of RD of 16 February 2016 (see paragraph 60). The name of the owner/keeper of the horses and the address of the collection point are recorded, in order to be able to send the invoice for rendering services. However, this data is not communicated to the CED, which as a result is unable to verify that owner/keepers are complying with their obligation to return the passport to the PIB. 15 c. The CA has not enforced the application of the requirements of the above- mentioned RD and, as a consequence, the numbers of the transponders of the horses rendered are not communicated to the CED (8). This is not in line with the requirements of Article 34 of Regulation (EU) 2015/262(9). d. In addition, there is no information available concerning the number of horses without identification. As a consequence, the CED is not reliable because many identifications of dead horses remain active in the CED. The fact that the identity of fallen stock is not recorded and that passports are not recuperated and destroyed jeopardises the credibility of the CED and leaves the door open to fraud.

The CCA stated that when a horse is slaughtered or dies in a different MS there is no uniformity in the way that feedback information is transmitted. The CCA has no means by which to evaluate if MS convey the information in all required cases. Sometimes: the CA of the other MS informs FASFC (who informs CBC); or they inform the PIB directly (who informs CBC); or no information is received. Exclusion of horses as food producing animals occurs in the following situations:

Belgian legislation requires notification to the CED of any changes regarding keepers and their contact details, yet such information is very rarely transmitted to the CBC for endorsement. 5.4.1.2 Identification verification (transponder) Dealers' premises and assembly centres

The evaluation of an animal's eligibility for slaughter is hindered by: a. The huge variety of model/templates of passports from different origins; b. The difficulties to consult foreign databases: e.g. the status of horses are not visible in certain databases (the Netherlands and Germany) c. The absence of information concerning the administration of essential substances and notification in the CED of changes in keepers as required by Belgian law. d. The absence of the date of identification in German passports, combined with the fact that the German database cannot be consulted. During transport

Any horse entering the country as part of intra-community trade is covered by a health certificate and is registered in TRACES. It must be registered in the CBC within 30 days and in any case before any change in keeper. Where no health certificate can be submitted to the CBC at the time of the registration request or where the health certificate is non-compliant, an approved veterinarian must perform a clinical examination of the animal and a blood sample is taken to test for the absence of specific diseases, such as Infectious anemia at the keeper's expense. In practice, very often the health certificate is kept by the first keeper (most commonly a dealer) and is not available to the owner requesting registration.

The content of the CED is not always up-to-date and its reliability is lessen due to various reasons, which also hinders its use for reconciliation and verification tasks. The CED contains 331,692 horses, but it is estimated by the CA that only 250,000 are still alive and present on the territory. The reasons for the discrepancies regarding information are: (11 ) In their response to the draft report, the CA noted that the CBC sends statistics on the evolution of data in Horse-ID to the FPS-HSFCE on a very regular basis (several times a year). The database is monitored indirectly: the FASFC inspection services regularly consult the data submitted. In the event of a problem, the information is sent to the FPS-HSFCE. This was the case before Horse-ID was introduced. Since the entry into force of this new programme, the tasks linked to the CBC have been carried out correctly. 20 a. Contrary to the provisions of Article 27 of Regulation (EU) 2015/262, there is delayed or absent notification of change of status by keepers, veterinarians and/or PIBs (horses that are excluded from the food chain, at a later stage, after registration, appear as eligible horses for the food chain in the database) and, contrary to Article 35 of the same Regulation, keepers are not returning the passports of dead horses to the PIBs. b. The CBC is not duly updated with information about fallen stock and for horses that have permanently left the country. As a consequence, a large number of dead horses are still active in the database (on average 10,000 dead horses are collected per annum by the rendering plant whereas the horse keepers do not return the passports back to the issuing bodies, contrary to what is required). Additionally there is no established flow of information from PIBs located in the other MS to where horses are permanently moved which, must transmit data updates to the central database of the MS where the animal was born/the passport was produced.
The different PIBs are not controlled by the CA and no checks are carried out to verify if the passports of dead animals are returned to the PIBs and if this information is included in the CED.

The CED records are based on the place of holding, not of the ownership. It records primarily identification information on horses that are kept in Belgium. There is an obligation for keepers to notify any change in contact details, end of holding period, place of holding if more than 90 days, permanent departure from the territory of Belgium, and exclusion from the food chain. However, keepers regularly omit to inform CED.

Under the provisions of the Memorandum of Agreement with the Netherlands, Luxembourg and France, registered horses may travel between these countries without being recorded in TRACES once they are accompanied by a passport, are microchipped and are fit and healthy to travel. If permanently resident in the new country, they must be registered at the CBC in the country of residence. However, communication of this new registration in other countries is seldom received by CED. Conclusions on horses identification, holdings/keepers registration and movement 21 controls

The fact that a number of horses are not yet identified, together with the late identification of horses after the compulsory period (12 months) highlight that the owners/keepers do not consistently meet their obligations on horse identification pursuant to Articles 11 and 12 of Regulation (EU) 2015/262. Nonetheless, the automatic exclusion from the food chain of horses which were registered late or for which duplicate or replacement passports were issued, mitigates potential risks in the production of horse meat.

The CED containing data of the registration and identification of horses is kept by the CBC at central level and is updated with information from the PIBs and the slaughterhouses. Even though the database allows for the recording of all the information required under EU rules, the information contained is not up to date, as relevant provisions (notably Articles 12, 27 and 35 of Regulation (EU) 2015/262) are not consistently adhered to.

The system in place does not provide reasonable assurance that the requirements laid down in Article 35 of Regulation (EU) 2015/262 are complied with and, in particular, concerning the obligation of the keeper of the deceased horses (excluding those slaughtered) to return the passport for invalidation by the PIBs.

citations.text: However, the audit team noted that the FNAO inspectors were not aware of the European guidance to verify how FBOs correctly take environmental samples to detect Listeria monocytogenes in their establishments. Supervision

However, staff was not aware of specific guidance regarding the FBO's methods for environmental sampling to detect Listeria monocytogenes, which therefore cannot be verified effectively by official controls. 5.2.2 Registration/approval of food establishments Legal requirements Article 6 of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004, Article 2 of Regulation (EU) No 210/2013 of the European Parliament and of the Council and Articles 10(2), 138(1), 138(2)(c)-(j), 138(3), 138(4) and 148 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Findings

The audit team noted that FNAO inspectors check if FBOs have environmental sampling in place to detect Listeria monocytogenes. However, the inspectors asked by the audit team did not witness how these own-control samples are taken in situ.

responses.response: An e-learning tool concerning Regulation (EU) No 2073/2005 with emphasis on Listeria monocytogenes (L.m) will be made available to the control staff. This tool will contain following parts: criteria for L.m., importance of growth characteristics of Ready to eat (RTE)-products in relation to growth of L.m., shelf life studies in general, shelf life studies for L.m. (based on literature, modelling, challenge testing, durability studies), environmental monitoring, analytical methods (incl. pooling). The official control staff will be made aware of the EU technical guidance document for shelf life studies for Listeria monocytogenes and the EU guidance document for the environmental sampling for Listeria monocytogenes. These documents are however currently under revision. As these new versions need to be included in the e-learning tool, the timeline for its completion will depend on the publication of the new version of these guidance documents. (see also audit General Follow-up, Reference Nr. 2020_6970, Recommendation 2019-6676-3)

recommendations.text: Ensure that the risk assessment takes into account different risk levels for different products, thus allowing official controls to adapt to risks, as required by Article 9(1)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

citations.text: The FASFC registration for primary producers of FNAO distinguishes between arable crops, fruit and vegetables. There is not more information available about the volume and nature of the production like soft fruit or leafy vegetables for direct consumption. There is a separate registration procedure for sprout producers in place (see below). Authorisation of processing plants
Different risk levels for different products, as indicated by EFSA5 opinions, have not been taken into account in the risk assessment.
Leafy green vegetables and soft berries are in the same risk category as potatoes and other vegetables intended to be eaten after cooking.
Frozen berries and frozen vegetables are in the same risk category as potatoes and other vegetables intended to be eaten after cooking.
In addition, for the risk based plan within the same product group, factors such as size of the farm/establishment and production volume are not taken into account.

The system is weakened by the fact that the information available about primary producers is insufficient to take into account higher risks of microbiological contamination of certain produce. This, and the fact that inspections regarding food hygiene do not comprise specific measures to prevent microbiological risks during the pre-harvest and harvest stages of production hamper the effectiveness of the official control system.

The system of own-controls certified by a recognised third party certification body in place could mitigate the risk of the lack of official controls before and during harvest. For primary producer's such own control systems are voluntary, and about 50% have certified own control systems in place.
As a result, different risk levels for different products are not taken into account, contrary to the provisions of Article 9 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

The LCU staff informed the audit team that official controls for primary producers focus on activities after harvest. Furthermore the LCU staff stated that the current registration system would not allow the inspectors to identify the size and the kind of crop produced at a farm. The only way to select farms with high risk crop would be by experience and former inspections carried out there.

Official controls are implemented as foreseen by the national control system. The official control system, however, is unable to identify and rectify shortcomings prior to and during harvesting of FNAO. 5.2.5 Official sampling Legal requirements 6 http://ec.europa.eu/food/audits-analysis/audit_reports/details.cfm?rep_id=4037 11 Articles 34 and 35 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 and Annex I, Chapter 1 of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005. recommendations.text: To complete and keep updated the MANCP with sufficient information regarding the objectives and official controls of the competent regional authorities in the animal welfare area. Legal basis for this recommendation: Articles 110(2) and 111(2) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625

citations.text: Belgium's 2018-2020 Multi-annual national control plan (MANCP) describes the protocol signed between FASFC and the three regions on delegation of responsibilities on animal welfare, providing the general framework. The MANCP (Section 3.2.11.15.6) states that the competent regional authorities undertake to periodically provide a contribution to MANCP and to the MANCP annual progress report. The audit team noted that information on the planning regarding animal welfare checks was very general, and it did not include objectives for animal welfare for any of the three regions. The MANCP is available at: http://www.afsca.be/apropos/mancp/mancpbelge/default.asp.

The 2018-2020 MANCP is incomplete regarding official controls in the animal welfare area. The absence of animal welfare objectives together with the absence of information from regional authorities to the progress report make it impossible to 10 assess whether the authorities are directing their efforts effectively or efficiently.

responses.response: he Regions will provide information regarding the objectives onal and official controls for the animal welfare area. We planned to get a definitive text to include in the MANCP for June 2021.

citations.text: The Flemish competent authority explained that, as FASFC is under the Federal competent authorities, it is difficult to cooperate without updating and improving the protocol signed with them. The Walloon competent authority agreed with that view and added that the non-optimal sharing of information with FASFC is mainly due to the institutional set up and they always try to achieve a good direct communication with the slaughterhouse official veterinarians.

The audit team requested an overview of the results of one of the points in the FASFC checklist from the Flemish competent authority. The competent authority indicated that, since 2018 the FASFC had not been entering the checklists into their electronic system, but instead sent either hard paper copies or e-mailed scanned copies to the regions. This makes it difficult for the regions to provide an overview and for their Animal Welfare Inspection Units to assess the findings. For this reason, the regions stopped using the FASFC findings for prioritising which slaughterhouses they visit.

The Flemish competent authority indicated that its Animal Welfare Unit has prepared new checklists and procedures. This is to prepare for the start of a new system where the Animal Welfare Unit would appoint directly private veterinarians to carry out inspections on animal welfare in slaughterhouses, in addition to the official veterinarians of the FASFC. This revision will take into account the non-compliances detected by veterinarians working in the slaughterhouse and prioritise the less compliant establishments for visits by the Animal Welfare Unit. The appointed private veterinarians will start at the end of October 2020. They will daily check animal welfare in every slaughterhouse for a maximum of three hours and they will complete the new checklist once a week per slaughterhouse.

The Walloon competent authority indicated that the shortage of resources limits their activities and for the time being they depend on the FASFC checks in the slaughterhouses and informed the audit team that: Its new plan is that its Animal Welfare Unit will do three controls per year for large scale slaughterhouses and one for the others. They did not provide a starting date. It has recently produced a new checklist for their Animal Welfare Unit. In March 2020, based on the protocol signed with FASFC, it issued new instructions for the FASFC official veterinarians.

The responsibilities for animal welfare at slaughter are clear, but Belgium has not ensured efficient and effective coordination between all authorities involved. This translates into suboptimal cooperation and insufficient sharing of information between the federal and regional competent authorities. The high dependence on the federal checks in the slaughterhouses is more relevant for the Walloon region, where the shortage of resources limits their activities. The checklists filled in by federal official veterinarians do not add much value to the official system. They systematically miss existing non-compliances and create administrative burden for regional authorities due to the way they are transmitted.

citations.text: In response to Recommendation 2 of audit report DG(SANTE) 2014-7057 - to take account of previous inspection results when establishing the risk basis for controls - the Belgian competent authorities provided in their action plan a summary of the system for controls in place after regionalisation, indicating that: Wallonia and Flanders analyse the reports of the FASFC official veterinarians to establish a benchmarking between slaughterhouses. That would allow the regions to prioritise certain slaughterhouses or specific items for their inspections.

The audit team noted that, for 2017, 2018 and 2019, there was no evidence that the analysis for benchmarking to prioritise between slaughterhouses had been carried out. The Flemish and Walloon authorities agreed that a systematic risk analysis had not been carried out in those years.

The slaughterhouse of Brussels-Capital region installed video cameras after the request from the regional competent authority following an animal welfare incident. The authority uses them (see paragraphs 26 to 28) to complement on-site inspections and to monitor critical points during slaughtering. The audit team noted that the regional competent authority officials have to review the recordings of the cameras on site. Due to the COVID-19 restrictions on on­site visits, they could not reach the frequency of video checks planned for the year. The animal welfare officer indicated that following the use of video footage, the staff performance, and the public image of the company have improved. 5.1.3 Controls on business operators' obligations Legal requirements Articles 5(1)(h), 12(1), 13, 14, 18(1), (2), (3), (4) of Regulation (EU) No 2017/625 Articles 4(1)(b), 11(3)(a), 24, 38, 39, 43(6), 44 and Annex I of Regulation (EU) No 2019/627 Articles 3(1)-(2), 4, 5(2)(c)(iv) and 5(3)(b), 7, 8(a), 13, 14 and Annex II Chapter I (3)(a) and (s), Chapter II (5) of Regulation (EU) No 2019/624 Articles 6 and 17 of Regulation (EC) No 1099/2009 8 Findings Brussels-Capital region

The absence of risk-based method for establishing the frequency for official controls does not allow the Flemish and Walloon competent authorities to set the frequency of their controls based on risk and to ensure the level of compliance expected in different situations. This decreases the efficiency of their official controls to target problematic establishments.

The measures that Brussels-Capital regional authority put in place in its red meat slaughterhouse paid off. They improved animal welfare, in particular during slaughter without stunning. The use of video surveillance by the operator and authorities proved useful to improve the welfare of animals and to enforce the legislation. The current arrangements where the officials can only review the video footage from the establishment is a lost opportunity for the authorities for e.g. keep their controls on the slaughterhouse during the Covid-19 restrictions.

citations.text: Audit report DG(SANTE) 2014-7059 recommended (Recommendation 7) setting up a procedure to ensure that the checks by a certifying body confirm that producers operating at the higher stocking densities comply with Directive 2007/43/EC.

In response to the pre-audit questionnaire for this audit, the competent authorities of the regions with broilers' farms (Flanders and Wallonia) indicated that they had signed a protocol with the certifying body. This protocol includes that this certifying body has to notify the Animal Welfare Units if it notices severe animal welfare infringements. The Animal Welfare Units will then follow up and carry out an inspection of its own.

The audit team noticed that: The certifying body provided a document of August 2020 with the items that they inspect and the way they carry out the inspections. In this document, the certifying body has grouped together, from the previous checklist, the animal welfare requirements laid down in Directive 2007/43/EC, to provide better information to the regional competent authorities and farmers. The two regional competent authorities have not yet analysed this document. The two regional competent authorities indicated that they do not have access to the database of the checklists completed by the certifying body and commented that if they had received the complete checklist, it would have been possible to see exactly which legislative requirements were not respected. The two regional competent authorities also informed the audit team that due to their heavy workload, the protocol with the certifying body has not been followed up properly and that they have not checked if the certifying body provides all the necessary data and that no analysis has been done. The last report that the certifying body sent to the regional competent authorities covered 2019. It includes all farms affiliated with the certifying body and the non- conformities the body found during its checks (mainly on stocking densities). The regional competent authorities' opinion is that the report provides insufficient information for them to carry out an analysis/assessment of compliance. There is no further guidance on what is considered "serious animal welfare 19 infringement". The certifying body has not issued any report of serious animal welfare deficiencies. Other items of the protocol signed with the certifying body were not implemented either, such as the yearly meetings to discuss follow up and the planned audits. All the above indicate there is little progress on setting up criteria for the use of increased stocking density and for the implementation of a procedure to ensure that the checks by a certifying body confirm that producers operating at the higher stocking densities comply with Annex V to Directive 2007/43/EC. Conclusions on criteria for the use of increased stocking density in broiler farms

The competent authorities have not addressed recommendation 7 of audit report DG (SANTE) 2014-7059. The absence of procedures to check compliance in producers operating at the higher stocking densities, together with the absence of monitoring signs of welfare problems at slaughterhouse level, leaves unmonitored the welfare of broilers from the farms presenting the greatest risks.

The protocol signed with the certifying body has not been implemented which leaves the regional competent authorities unaware of any possible shortcomings and welfare problems at farms. This impedes them to take effective action to solve existing issues.

The regional competent authorities cannot confirm compliance in the farms operating at the higher stocking densities. This creates the potential risk that broilers are kept at stocking densities under which the housing and management conditions are not able to ensure their welfare.

recommendations.text: To investigate all delays in getting laboratory results in order to prevent their recurrence. The national eradication plan and ASF diagnostic manual (Commission Decision 2003/422/EC)

citations.text: The competent authorities successfully strengthened surveillance in both domestic pigs and wild boars, notably in ASF restricted areas. The early detection system is now more effective and they have improved the monitoring of the epidemiological situation in the ASF infected area. However, the early detection system in ASF free areas is slightly weakened, in particular by not testing road killed wild boars and some non-investigated delays in turnaround times for getting laboratory results (3).

recommendations.text: To ensure that a special national health-mark is applied for fresh meat, meat preparations and meat products that are to be restricted to the national market, as required by Article 16 of Decision 2014/709/EU

citations.text: The authorities have not provided the additional guarantees required for meat derived from pigs originated in Part II and which is placed on the EU market (4); but until now, the associated risk has been limited. (2) In their response to the draft report the competent authority stated that the free areas are only permitted on condition that double fencing is installed for non-commercial pig farms. (3) In their response to the draft report the competent authority stated that the delays observed concern samples for which the veterinarian asks the first line laboratories DGZ and ARSIA for a certain diagnosis but without initially including ASF in the diseases to be analysed. After receipt of the analysis results, some veterinarians then request additional analyses on the same samples, sometimes including ASF in this additional demand. This is not in line with the competent authority instructions on increased surveillance for ASF, which require samples to be submitted to a first line laboratory for examination for ASF whenever treatment for a disease problem in a group of pigs is initiated. In the light of this finding the competent authority proposed actions to address the relevant recommendation (Rec no 1). (4) In their response to the draft report the competent authority stated that the practice of stamping the carcasses coming from part II with an oval EU health-mark, was already known prior the audit and an initiative was taken to change it - via a Royal Decree - and was already finalized. More of the modification of the Royal Decree of 19 March 2004 concerning the eradication of ASF, was modified on 5 December 2019 in order to provide the legislative basis for this national health mark. This practice has on this base immediately been stopped following the audit like foreseen. Since then, a special national health-mark has been used to stamp the carcasses of the few domestic pigs coming from part II. As before, these carcasses were only used for fresh meat sales in a supermarket in zone II (local distribution) and were not used for intracommunity trade. citations.text: The FPS-e is the central competent authority for controlling PDO/PGI/TSG products and GI spirit drinks on the market and their labelling in the entire country. DGEI inspectors of FPS-e are responsible for carrying out labelling and traceability checks at retailers and distribution centres of products under all national quality schemes including PDO/PGI/TSG products and GI spirit drinks. The vast majority are in response to complaints received, mainly concerning non- domestic products. Only a small part are carried out occasionally at randomly selected local markets and retailers. recommendations.text: Ensure that inspections of WPM subject to the WPM monitoring plan are carried out in line with Article 4(1) of Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/2125 to ensure compliance with Article 4(2) of the same regulation.

citations.text: The CA performs controls of WPM listed under Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2021/127, which is inspected at the BCPs at a rate of 15%, in line with the requirements of this Regulation. The CA stated that the wood packing material (WPM) monitoring plan is based on two pillars. Firstly, controls of WPM present in consignments subject to official control by FASFC at the BCP. Secondly, the CAs conduct checks on operators selected by the number of imported consignments of WPM imported from a list of combined nomenclature codes, when imported from; Canada, China, Democratic Republic of Korea, India, Japan, Mexico, Republic of Korea, Taiwan, USA and Vietnam, where the presence of Bursaphelenchus xylophilus and Anoplophora glabripennis is known. These checks are performed by the LCUs and target the WPM present at the operator during the visit, contrary to the requirements of Article 4(2) of Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/2125, which requires that these physical checks shall be carried out on consignments selected in accordance with the provisions of Article 4(1) of the same Regulation.

The monitoring plan for WPM identified as high risk by the CA, does not select specific consignments for inspection and as a result, may not effectively prevent the introduction of pests into the EU on these products.

responses.response: ion subject to amendment of legislation: Part of the WPM monitoring plan focuses on importers of risk material. These importers are selected on the basis of a customs lists of imported risk material. Imported consignments are usually delivered quickly at their destination. Directing these checks to imported consignments can only be put in place if their arrival is notified by a CHED-PP. Imposing such an obligation at national level would quickly result in a relocation of these imports to other Member States. Therefore, we propose to amend Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/2125 in such a way that monitoring of imported consignments is harmonised at EU level. Since the import requirements for WPM are harmonised at EU level, it would be logic that at all EU border control post product-origin combinations have the same chance to be checked.

The current monitoring plan of WPM of roducts not falling under the direct control of the Agency uses post-factum inspections at importers of risk material (e.g. WPM of construction materials, tiles...). In order to meet the recommendation, new additional checks on WPM of recently imported consignments of risk materials will be carried out at importers premises (place of destination). These recently imported consignments will be selected on the basis of monthly customs lists of imported consignments of risk material.

recommendations.text: The competent authority should ensure that appropriate enforcement measures are taken to ensure that operators remedy any non-compliance and prevent their reoccurrence as required by Article 138(1)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

citations.text: The audit team noted that, if the overall assessment is "Favourable" or "Favourable with comments", no corrective action is requested or enforced for identified non-compliance. This is only triggered if the inspections are "Unfavourable", which means that lower grade (less severe) non-compliances are up to the operators' discretion to address. This is not in line with Article 138(1)(b) of the OCR.

According to the CA, a new checklist has been developed designed to allow for the follow up of identified non-compliances, in order to prevent these being neglected and perpetuated. citations.text: In response to queries from the audit team in respect of the operation of the various official controls over operators working "under the approval" of an approval owner (option b(ii) above), the CA indicated these cases to be known, and fully within the scope of official controls: a) an applicant operator who plans to work with others in an "under the approval" arrangement, should indicate this on the floor plan with the approval application. b) All operators involved should be registered and have a registration number with an address of the establishment where the activity will take place. c) Operators that will work "under the approval" should apply to the LCU for approval using the application form, and in which they indicate whether they apply for approval or whether they intend to work "under the approval". d) The approval owner takes responsibility for the operators that work "under the approval" and will be subject to legal measures in case of non-compliance. (S)he is responsible both for the HACCP implementation, which the other operators must have access to and implement, as well as traceability. Concerning the latter, the records are kept either by the approval owner, or together with the other operators, but they must make arrangements for this. e) Legal measures can be taken against the approval owner if the activities of other operators working "under the approval" are not notified to the LCU. f) During an inspection, the CA will become aware of operators working "under the approval" and not complying with the requirements above.

The audit team noted that: a) Question 45 of the "Frequently asked questions" in the section on approvals on the CA website is only explicit in terms of time/space separation of activities and products for cases of individual approval of all operators involved. It is therefore unclear why a prospective approval owner would need to indicate the intention to operate a working "under the approval" arrangement on the floor plan. Moreover, such an arrangement may be entered into at any time, even after the approval. 9 b) Although the approval application requires operators to indicate their intent to work "under the approval", it does not require an attestation or acknowledgement from the approval owner as regards the obligations arising from this arrangement. c) According to the CA, legal measures against operators not complying with the requirements can only be taken if these operators are present and produce, during an official control (4).

The audit team noted a case of an approved establishment known to the CA to have four operators working "under the approval" arrangements, and of which the CA had sought the withdrawal of the approval. The official control reports drafted did not include references to non-compliances identified in relation to the activities of these four operators, but do not clarify whether this was because they were compliant, or because they were not present and active during the official controls. Upon request by the audit team, the CA performed an official control in order to verify whether progress has been made towards compliance of the operator, during which two additional operators were identified on site, working "under the approval", and which were not known to the CA, as neither had submitted the required application to the LCU. Therefore, the CA was also not aware how long these operators had been active under this arrangement.

The provision to allow operators to produce in approved establishments "under the approval" of another operator, and the way this is implemented, has a negative impact on ability of the control system to verify and ensure compliance with the legal requirements of all operators involved and, consequently, on the safety, hygiene and traceability of fishery products produced by those operators under such an arrangement.
