audits.title: One Health - Highly pathogenic avian influenza

recommendations.text: Awareness and prevention 25. In Belgium regional environmental authorities are the competent authorities for wildlife manage- ment including wildlife health and biodiversity: a) Agentschap Natuur en Bos in Flanders, b) (Département de la Nature et des Forêts) in Wallonia, c) (Leefmilieu Brussel) in Brussels. 26. Regional environmental authorities provide information on their website for the public on HPAI risks and what to do when they find a dead wild bird or animal. There is a citizens' magazine where regional environmental authorities can communicate information on appropriate precau- tions. 27. Members of the public can report wildlife carcasses through a free national hotline in Belgium, with an additional regional hotline available for Wallonia. They will be advised whether the car- cass should be sent for testing (if it qualifies for surveillance testing). If the carcass is found on municipal land and qualifies for surveillance testing then the regional environmental authority will be involved in the dispatch fo the carcasses to the NRL. The municipalities are responsible for disposal of the remaining carcass (if any) or of a carcass found on their land if it is not qualified 8 for surveillance testing. They are also responsible for providing the appropriate protective measures such as PPE to their staff handling the carcass. If the carcass is found on private land the regional environmental authority will also dispatch it to the NRL if it qualified for surveillance testing. If it does not, then the owner must dispose of the carcass with no other intervention by the authorities and is responsible for appropriate PPE. There is no communication to people that have found a wildlife carcass in the case of it testing positive for HPAI. 28. In Belgium there are several wildlife sanctuaries and rehabilitation centres. Regional authorities are also responsible for these wildlife rehabilitation centrrs and provide derogations to these cen- tres in order for them to capture, transport, temporarily accommodate (rehabilitate) endemic wild- life species (i.e. species listed on the Soortenbesluit in Flanders, Natuurordonnantie for Brussels Capital Region). Some can host up to 4,000 birds and small mammals (rabbits, foxes, squirrels) annually, and keep young animals for several months. Injured, sick or distressed wild animals found by the public are consistently directed towards these centres. Flanders has legislation in place to recognize wildlife rehabilitation centres. A significant proportion of their staff are volun- teers. PPE and training on its use is the responsibility of the employer i.e. the wildlife rehabilitation centres. The biosecurity, with respect to inter-animal transmission, is the responsibility of the re- gional environmental authorities.

Monitoring & early detection 29. The environmental authorities have not carried out a specific risk assessment or developed a risk mitigation policy for the potential effects of Avian Influenza on wildlife and biodiversity. Scientific risk assessments are performed from RAG-V-EZ or the FASFC. However, the Research Institute for Nature and Forest (INBO), an independent research institute of the Flemish government, closely follows up the outbreaks of Avian Influenza in the Flanders (in collaboration with ANB). 30. The HPAI epidemiological situation elsewhere in Europe is monitored by veterinary services at federal level and by the regional environmental authorities through information disseminated by neighbouring countries and European bodies. These include, for example, the website of the EU reference laboratory, EFSA's quarterly reports and dashboard (https://hpai.efsa.aus.vet/), information disseminated by the European Commission and Member States via mail and at PAFF meetings, initiatives such as bird flu radar (https://app.bto.org/mmt/avian_influenza_map/avian_influenza_map.jsp), following webinars and conferences with HPAI topics. 31. In 2006, in response to the risks associated with the introduction of zoonotic H5N1 viruses from Asia by migratory birds, Belgian veterinary authorities conducted a risk assessment regarding high-risk zones and wetlands for migratory waterfowl. As a result of this evaluation, so-called "sensitive natural areas" were identified. These are wetlands where large numbers of waterfowl reside, with high numbers of migratory waterfowl passing through, resting, and foraging each year. Because of the change in epidemiological evidence regarding HPAI virus, a new evaluation should be carried out to identify sensitive natural areas. In these areas, FASFC imposes specific measures on poultry establishments and specific attention is given by the regional environmental authorities 9 to the surveillance in wild birds. The visit team saw evidence of several poultry and livestock farms located directly under the paths of wild migratory birds close to wetlands. 32. In areas where hunting of waterfowl or other animals is permitted (Wallonia and Flanders), regional environmental authorities may impose measures to either ban hunting or enforce stricter regulations in case of HPAI presence in the area. For example, in 2022, this was the case at three locations in Wallonia, where a high infection rate of HPAI was detected in pheasants and ducks that had been released for hunting. 33. For birds released for hunting, responsibilities for managing HPAI risks are divided between the veterinary and the regional environmental services. Until their release, these birds are considered captive birds; once released, they are considered as wild birds. Often, these birds are imported from another member state (France). They are not included in the active surveillance whereas there have been three HPAI outbreaks in Wallonia involving thousands of these birds. As these birds can further infect other wildlife upon their release, a risk assessment for better managing possible HPAI risks to exposed humans, other wildlife and poultry, appropriate measures and a clear division of responsibilities may be important to consider. The practice is banned in the regions of Flanders and Brussels. 34. There is wastewater surveillance for monitoring influenza in some stations in Wallonia but not targeting HPAI.

Actions and guidance regarding initial response to HPAI cases 35. Regional environmental services are communicating with the NRL and veterinary authorities in the context of positive wildlife samples. The authorities in their comments to the draft report stated that the regional environmental authorities communicate the necessary information on the findings received from the NRL towards the FASFC, the concerned municipalities, the other regional environmental authorities and respective regional health authorities. The team however did not see an established communication channel for timely warning to public health authorities in the event of wildlife deaths due to HPAI. 36. Regional environmental authorities are currently members of the joint structure RAG-V-EZ that is established with the FASFC to assess and manage HPAI risks. Their participation in such a multisectoral structure facilitates the flow of information regarding the HPAI risks during outbreaks in farms. III. Human health 1. Awareness and prevention 37. The national competent authority for public health is the Federal Public Service of health at Federal level and at regional level the Department Zorg for Flanders, the Agence pour une vie de qualité for Wallonia and Vivalis for Brussels. 38. There is the RMG (multidisciplinary, with federal and regional health authorities and designated scientific experts including epidemiologists) that meets and communicates on an ad hoc basis 10 regarding the management of Avian Influenza risks for public health, such as guidance for PPE for health professionals. Communication flows from the RMG to both primary and secondary care sectors, with the primary care sector receiving information through federal public health entities. 39. There is also the RAG at federal level that is composed of designated scientists (bringing in additional specialists from specific areas depending on the subject) that carries out risk assessments and issues recommendations on a scientific basis. It was created (in place since 2008) to be independent and is an advisory body. 40. Another working group with risk assessment output of advisory nature is the RAG-V-EZ which has a more veterinary focus and was described under the animal health section. In 2023 it issued an opinion on the zoonotic risks of Avian Influenza virus infections in mammals with its recommendations summarised in an FAQ format, publicly available on the FASFC website4. In this context the group was requested to provide advice in the first case of mammal infection in a farm (ferrets in 2023). However, the study team found that although the advice of RAG-V-EZ is in the public domain, relevant at-risk groups such as private and local government veterinarians were not aware of their existence. Hence authorities could consider improving the visibility and communication channels of the RAG-V-EZ to allow its advice to reach relevant professional groups at operational level. 41. As both RAG and Rag-V-EZ groups have competencies in zoonotic diseases there seems to be an overlap in some aspects of their scope (e.g. occupational health). Further clarification of scopes and relevant processes would enhance the clarity of the necessary advice and communication channels. 42. The Superior Health Council of Belgium issues annual guidelines for seasonal influenza vaccination, identifying priority groups based on risk factors. These groups typically include individuals at higher risk of complications, such as pregnant women, people aged 65 and over, those with chronic conditions, and healthcare personnel. 43. The Council has not specifically included poultry workers and veterinarians in the priority groups for the national strategy for seasonal flu, citing a lack of clear evidence to support their inclusion. The recommended prioritisation was nevertheless requested by the RAG-V-EZ, also in line with the HSC opinion on zoonotic Avian Influenza, by the time of the audit. 44. Occupational health services are based at federal level and have limited involvement in ensuring appropriate PPE use at workplaces with high risk of HPAI exposure. The RAG-V-EZ has provided advice in relation to appropriate protective equipment, and precautions to reduce spillover risks from zoonotic avian influenza for people exposed to potentially infected animals. The responsibility for the PPE supply and use lies with the employer. Subcontracting firms undertaking culling, cleaning and disinfection on infected farms are providing their staff with PPE and training on appropriate use. Some of these firms can be based in a different Member State. Compliance with relevant occupational health requirements in this case, lies with the Member State where the firm is based. The team saw evidence of mostly appropriate PPE and correct use from staff of 4 https://favv-afsca.be/nl/themas/dieren/dierengezondheid/dierziekten/vogelgriep (in Dutch) 11 these firms although it also saw evidence of no mask wearing during depopulation of infected farms. 45. While there is no vaccination program specifically for Avian Influenza, there is a strategic stockpile of Avian Influenza vaccines (Bavarian). The Belgian Task Force Therapeutics Viral Diseases has evaluated antiviral agents like oseltamivir (Tamiflu®) and baloxavir (Xofluza®) for potential stockpiling in preparation for influenza pandemic. 46. There is no generalized awareness campaign directed at the public concerning Avian Influenza spillover risks from birds and mammals. Health authorities have determined that such a campaign could lead to unnecessary panic and potentially undermine public trust in health guidance. This has been agreed upon multiple times as a consensus among Belgian health authorities. Information on the zoonotic risks of HPAI can be found nevertheless the website of FASFC and environmental authorities. 2. Monitoring & early detection 47. The laboratory of respiratory pathogens at Viral Diseases of Sciensano acts as the National Influ- enza Centre in Belgium and is officially recognized by the WHO and ECDC. Overall, Sciensano is ISO 17025 accredited for more than 100 different test procedures. In 2012, several laboratories, including the laboratory of respiratory viruses, obtained the ISO 15189 accreditation for different test methods. 48. It is coordinating the national surveillances programs for influenza including influenza like illness (ILI) (since 2007) and Severe Acute Respiratory Infections surveillance (SARI) (since 2010) thereby testing for influenza (typing and subtyping) and 16 other respiratory viruses. 49. Samples from the sentinel networks of the above surveillance programs (hospitals, general practi- tioners, nursing homes) and from external laboratories/hospitals are submitted to a series of tests: identification and typing for influenza A and B, subtyping influenza A (for H1, H3, N1 and N2), determination of influenza B lineage (Yamagata, Victoria) and subtyping for H5Nx, H7Nx, H9Nx for suspected cases of avian flu (by qPCR, but WGS has been also implemented) and swine influ- enza is performed on samples that test negative for seasonal influenza virus and if there is any indication of a zoonotic event. Results are shared with the RAG and with ECDC weekly. 50. A subset of influenza positive clinical samples is sequenced at the laboratory to characterize cir- culating strains to detect mutations in the hemagglutinin (HA) and neuraminidase (NA) genes which might be associated with severe clinical outcomes. A subset of samples is isolated and fur- ther characterized (e.g. hemagglutination inhibition test and sero-neutralisation). Results are shared with RAG and ECDC weekly. The Centre notifies ECDC (through the European surveil- lance portal for infectious diseases, Epipulse) of confirmed cases within 24 hours of laboratory diagnosis. Results are also shared with WHO and ECDC twice a year. 51. The Centre shares data with the WHO Global Influenza Surveillance and Response System Collaborating Centres for Reference and Research on Influenza. It is also responsible for uploading 12 genetic sequencing data on influenza virus in the Global Initiative on Sharing All Influenza Data (GISAID).

audits.title: Avian influenza – Implementation of prevention and control measures

recommendations.text: To ensure that registration requirements exclude only the birds' establishments that pose an insignificant risk to the epidemiology of avian influenza in the country, as laid down in Article 85 of Regulation (EU) 2016/429.

Article 4 (27), 84 and 85 of Regulation (EU) 2016/429 and Article 3 of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2022/1345. Recommendation based on main conclusion No. 54 and nsure that official laboratories carrying out the laboratory analyses, tests and diagnoses on samples taken during official controls and other official activities, in the context of the detection of a disease for surveillance purposes, are designated, and either accredited for the methods used, according to Art 37 (4) of the Regulation (EU) 2017/625, or, if applicable, fulfil the requirements for the derogation under Art 40 (1) (b) of that Regulation.4 Articles 2 (2), Article 37, and 40 (1) (b) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Recommendation based on main conclusion No. 59 and

citations.text: Belgian legislation (Royal decrees of 5 May 2008 and of 20 May 2022) requires mandatory registration of: i. all commercial poultry establishments regardless of the number of birds kept, ii. all poultry traders, iii. all "hobby keepers" with more than 200 hobby poultry, 4 iv. and all "hobby keepers" who wish to participate in or trade hobby poultry through public events such as a local weekly market. So called "hobby keepers" with less than 200 birds can attend competitions or exhibitions without having to register, and can sell directly to other hobby keepers, but if they supply the food chain or are involved in any commercial activities they must also be registered. In the event of participating in a public gathering, their identity details must be recorded by the event organiser.

"Hobby poultry" is defined in a guidance document for the public as the most common poultry species, including chicken, ducks, turkeys etc that are not intended for the food chain or for restocking supplies of game; they are then considered to be "captive birds". This definition, and the national provisions applied, are not entirely in line with the Animal Health Law (AHL), which defines poultry as birds kept or reared in captivity for production (of eggs, meat or other products). Furthermore, Articles 84 and 85 of Regulation (EU) 2016/429 and Article 3 of Commission Implementing Regulation 2022/1345, which provides for exceptions for registration of establishments, require among other that the kept terrestrial animals, germinal products or products of animal origin on the establishments, are not intended to be moved out of the establishment.

In Belgium there are several wildlife rehabilitation centres (around 25) which shelter injured or abandoned animals until they can be released into the wild again. The audit team interviewed a manager of one of these centres, located near the coast. The capacity of that centre could reach up to of approximately 5,000 birds annually. In some cases, the centre can keep birds for up to few months, especially when dealing with young birds, before they can be released in the wild again. These centres are currently not registered with veterinary authorities, despite keeping birds for an extended period and 5 therefore falling under the definition of an establishment according to Article 4 (27) of the AHL. citations.text: When a farm veterinarian notifies the suspicion, authorities instruct the private veterinarian to take samples and to carry out the clinical assessment of the birds present at the establishment. The audit team noted a case, when the private veterinarian had a suspicion during his animal health check visit, and therefore took samples based on a general instruction document (available at the FASFC website) and sent them to a regional laboratory for further dispatch to the NRL. The practitioner then informed the LCU of the suspicion by email, including a clinical assessment of the animals present, as requested by Article 6 (2) of Delegated Regulation 2020/687. During the audit, the competent authority could not state clearly whether they reserve these tasks for an official veterinarian or they are officially delegated to private veterinarians according to Article 28 of the Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

LCUs contact registered establishments in the restricted zones, asking them to do an inventory of birds kept and to send it back, in the protection zone within 24 hours and in the surveillance zone within 48 hours. They also contact mayors asking them to forward publish information on restriction measures on local channels, to ensure that hobby keepers that are not registered receive information. All commercial establishments within the protection zone are visited by their private veterinarians within 24 hours. During these visits the veterinarians perform clinical examinations, checking health and production parameters' records, and taking samples for laboratory analysis as necessary. 17

The restriction zones established following an outbreak of HPAI are lifted as follows: i. The protection zone is lifted 21 days after it is established, provided hat clinical examinations on commercial holdings within the zone--conducted every four days--show no signs of concern. Once lifted, the area becomes part of the surveillance zone. ii. The surveillance zone is lifted 30 days after it is established, provided that no new outbreaks have been detected and all registered poultry establishments have undergone clinical examinations by a farm veterinarian and sampling as per FASFC instructions. The zone is lifted once all samples collected have been favourably tested using PCR testing by DGZ or Sciensano.

audits.title: Slaughter hygiene and meat inspection requirements

recommendations.text: To ensure that own-check sampling programmes implemented by food business operators comply with Article 5 of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005, in particular, to ensure that: · the national provisions are in line with EU requirements; · food business operators` compliance with the requirements laid down in Article 5(5) of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005, are verified during official controls.

citations.text: However, the audit team noted that the Royal Decree (RD) of 30 November 2015 on the hygiene of foodstuffs of animal origin states that Food Business Operators (FBOs) of slaughterhouses of domestic ungulates should take their own-check carcass samples "at the end of the slaughter line or in the chiller but in any case, within two to four hours after slaughter".

As a result, the audit team noted in the four domestic ungulates' large capacity slaughterhouses visited that FBOs took these samples within two to four hours after slaughter when the carcasses already underwent blast-chilling. This is not in line with the provisions of Chapter II of Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005 which requires that such samples should be taken after dressing but before chilling. Article 5(5) of the mentioned Regulation allows that FBOs may use other sampling and testing procedures, if they can demonstrate to the satisfaction of the CA that these procedures provide at least equivalent guarantees. The FASFC confirmed to the audit team that no such study had been carried out so far in order to provide the required guarantees.

National legislation and guidelines, necessary to ensure implementation and/or enforcement of the EU requirements applicable to the meat sector, are in place and they largely ensure compliance with EU legislation, except for some provisions regarding the own-check sampling of carcasses.

The audit team noted that the analytical method used by the FBOs are not consistently verified during official controls. In some cases, it was neither clear from the FBOs procedures nor from the analytical results whether the reference method or an alternative method was used by the FBO. Moreover, some of the LCU inspectors informed the audit team that they do not verify if the analytical method used by the FBO was in line with the requirements of points 1 and 5 of Article 5 of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005 and/or were not aware of the availability of the list of the validated methods on the CA`s website. They were satisfied with the fact that the laboratory performed the analyses was accredited.

The official control system in place also includes taking official samples for microbiological analyses in order to guarantee the safety of red meat and poultry meat. However, the effectiveness of the system is weakened by the inconsistencies noted by the audit team in relation to CA` verification of FBOs` compliance with microbiological criteria.

recommendations.text: To ensure that post-mortem inspection is carried out in accordance with EU legislation. In particular, to ensure that all incisions, required under Article 19 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627, are performed during post-mortem inspection of bovine animals.

citations.text: Although the audit team was provided with evidence of VOAs` training in all slaughterhouses visited and noted that procedures are available which describe the palpations and incisions that must be made during the PMI, non-compliances with Articles 19, 20 and 23 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627 were noted by the audit team in the slaughterhouses of domestic ungulates visited (see more under paragraph 65).

The mechanisms in place (such as documented procedures, training, and several IT applications) give the CAs a reasonable level of assurance that controls are carried out uniformly and consistently. However, the staff knowledge in relation to implementation of PMI requirements, which suggest a need for further training, does not ensure that the PMI requirements are apply fully in line with the EU requirements.

Although training and guidance documents are available to the VOAs performing PMI, the audit team noted some deficiencies in relation to the implementation of PMI in most of the slaughterhouses for ungulates visited: · pig testicles were not subject to visual inspection as required by point 1(h) of Article 23 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627, · masseters of adult bovines were not systematically incised (only one incision in the external masseter instead of the required two) as required by point 1(a) of Article 19 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627, · the lymph nodes (i.e. retropharyngeal, bronchial, and mediastinal) of adult bovines were not systematically incised as required by points 1(a) and 1(b) of Article 19 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627, · the bovine udder was not inspected as required by point 1(k) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627 · These shortcomings were not detected by the AR-VOA or the LCU inspector (in a small capacity slaughterhouse visited, a LCU inspector was not familiar with the details of the required PMI procedure).

In addition, in a small slaughterhouse implementing the derogation on the timing of PMI, the PMI of the gastro-intestinal tract was not carried out properly as the VOA carried out such inspection in small buckets/bins that did not allow a proper inspection (only a small surface of the tract was visible).

In general, AMI both for domestic ungulates and poultry and PMI of poultry are organised in line with the relevant EU requirements. However, the implementation of PMI has some systemic shortcomings, in particular, related to the obligatory incisions to be made during PMI of bovine animals (see also paragraph 48).

recommendations.text: To ensure that, when a non-compliance is established, the competent authority takes appropriate measures so that the operator concerned remedies the non- compliance and prevents reoccurrence of same as required by Article 138 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. 19

citations.text: The CCA informed the audit team that follow up of non-compliances detected during inspections where the result is "favourable with remarks" is carried out during the next planned inspection visit by the LCU inspector. In these cases, no deadline for correction is given to the FBO and the non-compliances are expected to be corrected by the following CA visit (which can be in 3 or 6 months depending on the planned inspection frequency). Although the VOAs are permanently present at the slaughterhouses, the FASFC procedure does not require them to perform such follow up controls.

The audit team also noted some inconsistencies regarding the deadlines given to rectify non-compliances which could have been eliminated by an immediate action, in order to comply with the requirements of Article 137(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. In two slaughterhouses visited the deadlines given to the FBO to remedy the issues related to knife sterilisers (insufficient contact time with the disinfectant used to sterilize knives) was around two months (in one of the cases the deadline was extended). In other slaughterhouses an immediate action was requested by the LCU inspector in similar situations.

The system in place provides official staff with legal powers for the performance of 9 official controls and the enforcement of legal requirements. However, the enforcement system is weakened by the fact that some non-compliances are not always followed up in a manner which ensures swift corrective action by the FBO.

audits.title: Official Import Controls

recommendations.text: To ensure that in the case of consignments of goods of animal origin in transit: a. identity checks are performed in line with relevant EU requirements; b. goods of animal origin in transit to vessels located in ports in other Mem- ber States are accompanied by a duly completed official certificate in ac- cordance with the model laid down in Part I of the Annex to the Imple- menting Regulation (EU) 2019/2128; c. goods of animal origin in transit to vessels located in third countries are accompanied by a duly completed and finalised common health entry document, and d. the competent authority at approved warehouses takes appropriate measures when it does not receive confirmation of arrival of consign- ments of goods of animal origin transported to vessels leaving the Union. Legal requirements: Article 49(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, Article 3(1) and (2) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/2130, Articles 26(4)(a) and (b), 30 and 31(5) of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/2124, and Articles 5, 28(a) and (b) and Part 2 of the Annex to Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/2128. To ensure that the border control posts, inspection centres thereof and control points comply with the minimum requirements for the categories of goods for which the post has been designated and are only listed if compliant with those requirements.

citations.text: The audit team noted, according to data in TRACES-NT for 2024, that in the vast ma- jority (over 90%) of cases of consignments in transit, confirmation of arrival and compli- ance of consignments had been completed in part III of the relevant CHEDs at either the BCPs of exit or the approved warehouses. However, at the warehouse visited, the audit team observed that the identity check on arrival of consignments at this warehouse was mainly based on information provided by the operator rather than the performance of an identity check, which was not in line with Article 26(4)(a) and (b) of Delegated Regula- tion (EU) 2019/2124 nor has the FASFC exempted consignments from those checks or updated its procedures to allow the derogation provided in Article 27(3) of the same Regulation.

For consignments of goods of animal origin in transit to United States' army bases locat- ed in the EU, the staff at one BCP allow the identity checks to be carried out based in part by information provided by the terminal operator on such consignments. This prac- tice is not in line with Article 49(1) of the OCR and Article 3(1) and (2) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/2130.

Regarding the evaluated cases of consignments of goods in transit to vessels located in ports in other Member States, the audit team noted that an official certificate in accord- ance with the model laid down in Part I of the Annex to Commission Implementing Reg- ulation (EU) 2019/2128 had been issued in each case. The certificates, however, were not always completed in line with the requirements set out in Article 5 and Part 2 of the An- nex to Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/2128.

At one BCP, the arrival of the consignments of goods in transit to vessels had not been confirmed for the 25 certificates issued in 2024 and follow-up measures were not ap- plied, which is not in line with Articles 30 and 31(5) of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/2124, although BCP staff had sent several reminders to the warehouse operator.

The audit team further noted that the FASFC did not ensure that the warehouse operator did submit a CHED in TRACES-NT for consignments transported from the warehouse to exit BCPs to be delivered to supply vessels in ports in third countries, and consequently failed to authorise the movement by finalising the CHEDs which must accompany con- signments. This is not in line with Article 28(a) and (b) of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/2124. The competent authorities instead issued an official certificate in accordance with the model laid down in Part I in the Annex to Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/2128. 5.2.4 Documentary, identity and physical checks of consignments 5.2.4.1 Checks on consignments of animals

The FASFC stated that, with the exception mentioned in finding 30, identity checks are full checks or limited to a check on the seals on containers or means of transport in line with Article 3(1) and (2) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/2130.

The official controls on animals and goods entering the EU through BCPs in Belgium are generally carried out in line with relevant EU legislation, documented procedures and planned arrangements. However, some shortcomings were noted in the performance of official controls on consignments of goods of animal origin in transit, which potentially weaken the guarantee that only compliant goods enter the Union.

recommendations.text: Legal requirements: Articles 53(1)(a), 62(1), 63(1) and 64(3)(b), (h) and (i) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 and Articles 3(1)(a), (b) and (c), (2) and (3), 4(2)(a) and 8(2) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/1014.

citations.text: The audit team noted that seven inspection centres visited as part of the BCPs Antwerp Port, Brussels airport and Zeebrugge Port, of which three inspection centres were also designated as control points, were not compliant with certain minimum requirements for BCPs laid down in Articles 53(1)(a) and Article 64(3) of the OCR, and Articles 3, 4 and 8(2) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/1014, for the categories of goods for which they had been designated.

The audit team noted the following non-compliances at these seven inspection centres, which, with one exception, remained undetected or were not recorded in the FASFC con- trol reports: · there was no room for storage of frozen goods of non-animal origin at the inspection centre Keurpunt at the BCP Antwerp Port, which is not in line with Article 3(1)(c) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/1014. · unloaded at about 12 meters from the facilities, the walls of the facilities are not 14 easy to clean and disinfect, part of the walls were not maintained, and inspection equipment was not kept clean, which is not in line with Articles 53(1)(a) and 64(3)(h) of the OCR and Article 3(1)(a) and (c), and (2) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/1014. · the facilities for unloading and storage of goods of animal origin not intended for human consumption at the inspection centre NHC-dnata Belgium at the BCP Brus- sels Airport were not easy to clean and disinfect and were not kept clean, which is not in line with Article 64(3)(h) of the OCR and Article 3(1)(c) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/1014. · the size of the facilities at the inspection centre Worldwide Flight Service Belgium nv at the BCP Brussels Airport was not suitable for the volume of goods of animal origin handled at this inspection centre, which is not in line with Article 64(3)(b) of the OCR. The BCP staff informed the audit team that this issue was identified during its verification visits, resulting in three administrative sanctions. The staff stated that a subsequent verification visit with findings of non-compliance may lead to the sus- pension of activities of this inspection centre for this category of goods. · the BCP staff provided the audit team with reports of recent verification visits in which it reported non-compliances identified, along with corrective actions taken, at the inspection centre Eurofruitports at the BCP Antwerp Port. The audit team, how- ever, identified the following additional findings regarding operational hygiene and maintenance of the facilities, which are not in line with Articles 53(1)(a) and 64(3)(h) and (i) of the OCR and Articles 3(3) and 4(2)(a) of Implementing Regula- tion (EU) 2019/1014: o The unloading, inspection and storage areas were poorly maintained and not clean or easy to clean o The inspection area was not equipped with a table with a smooth washable surface easy to clean and disinfect. o The inspection area contained a storage cabinet with equipment both of which were dirty.

The audit team visited one control point designated by the competent authority for the performance of identity and physical checks on consignments of plants and noted that it was not compliant with the minimum requirements for BCPs, which is not in line with Articles 53(1)(a) and 64(3)(h) and (i) of the OCR, and Article 3(1)(b), (2) and (3) of Im- plementing Regulation (EU) 2019/1014 for the following reasons: · A container used for storage of quarantined goods, and the area surrounding it, were not maintained and kept clean. · Part of the fittings (racking) in a storage area for detained consignments were rusty and therefore not easy to clean. · One of the two inspection areas was not clean or maintained and easy to clean and did not have a supply of hot and cold running water. The competent authorities stat- 15 ed that it did not allow use of the exemption laid down in Article 3(6)(a) of Imple- menting Regulation (EU) 2019/1014. Conclusions on the compliance of border control posts with minimum requirements

The BCPs, including inspection centres thereof, and the control points visited were, with two exceptions, not compliant with certain minimum requirements for BCPs for the cate- gories of goods for which they had been designated. Consequently, the Belgian authorities cannot guarantee that compliant facilities are in place for the proper handling of goods and the prevention of risks which may result from cross-contamination.

audits.title: to evaluate the implementation of official controls on medicated feed

recommendations.text: To ensure that veterinary prescriptions and labels for medicated feed shall contain and comply with all information set out in the relevant legal requirements.

citations.text: The audit team scrutinised documentation of FeBOs on manufacturing medicated feeds in all visited establishments. In general, prescriptions, recipes and labels of medicated feeds were available. The audit team randomly assessed prescriptions of different medicated feeds and in all cases, the prescriptions did not contain information on percentage of medicated feed in the daily ration or quantity of medicated feed per animal per day, and warnings necessary to ensure the proper use. This is not in line with the requirements of points 11 and 13 of Annex V to Regulation (EU) 2019/4. These were overlooked during previous official controls.

The audit team randomly assessed labels or accompanying documents of different medicated feeds and in several cases, labels did not contain information on contra- indications, instructions for use in line with the veterinary prescription and the withdrawal periods. This is not in line with the requirements of points 4, 5 and 8 of Annex III to Regulation (EU) 2019/4.

In general, the inspection planning system is based on appropriate risk-related factors and thus ensures that the official controls are carried out on all operators regularly, on a risk basis and with appropriate frequency. However, the effectiveness of the official controls system is weakened by shortcoming in the competent authority's assessment of completeness of prescriptions and labels of medicated feed. 7 5.2.2 Sampling 5.2.2.1 Planning of official sampling
